qs.e: Camphor sublimes. So do naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice. Ice and wax melt first.

qs.q: The process in which a solid turns into a gas without becoming a liquid is called:
qs.e: Sublimation: solid → gas directly. The reverse (gas → solid) is deposition.

qs.q: Dry ice is the solid form of:
qs.e: Dry ice is solid CO₂. It sublimes at about −78.5 °C, leaving no liquid behind — hence 'dry'.

qs.q: In which state of matter is diffusion fastest?
o: It is the same in all
qs.e: Gas particles move fastest and have the most space, so a smell spreads through a room quickly.

qs.q: Plasma is known as the ______ state of matter.
qs.e: Solid, liquid, gas are the first three; plasma (ionised gas, as in the Sun and lightning) is the fourth; BEC the fifth.

qs.q: The Bose–Einstein Condensate is formed by cooling matter to:
qs.e: BEC forms at temperatures within a fraction of a degree of 0 K. It was predicted by S. N. Bose and Albert Einstein.

Clay is a good conductor of heat

qs.q: Steam at 100 °C causes more severe burns than boiling water at 100 °C because steam has:

o: Water boils at a lower temperature where air pressure is low
Water boils at a higher temperature
There is less oxygen to burn the fuel
qs.e: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point of water, so the water is not hot enough to cook quickly. A pressure cooker raises the boiling point.

o: Raises its boiling point and lowers its freezing point

qs.q: The heat absorbed when a solid changes into a liquid at its melting point, without a rise in temperature, is called:

qs.q: Which of these does NOT increase the rate of evaporation?
qs.e: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so evaporation slows down.

qs.q: Gases are easy to compress because:

qs.e: Large gaps between gas particles let them be squeezed together — that is why LPG and CNG can be stored in cylinders.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT an example of sublimation?
qs.e: Butter melts into a liquid. The other three go straight from solid to vapour.

qs.q: Water drops forming on the outside of a glass of ice-cold water is due to:
qs.e: Water vapour in the air cools on touching the cold glass and condenses into droplets.

qs.q: Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is found in:
qs.e: Plasma is a hot ionised gas — in the Sun, stars, lightning, neon and fluorescent tubes.

qs.q: The boiling point of water at normal atmospheric pressure is:
qs.e: 100 °C = 373 K. The melting point of ice is 273 K.

qs.q: The Indian scientist after whom 'bosons' are named is:

qs.q: Which of the following is a compound?
qs.e: Water (H₂O) has hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio with new properties. Air, brass and sea water are mixtures.

qs.q: Air is a:
qs.e: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, CO₂ and other gases in varying amounts.

qs.q: Brass is an example of a:
qs.e: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc — a homogeneous mixture (solid solution), not a compound.

qs.q: Which method is used to separate the different coloured dyes in an ink?
qs.e: Chromatography separates dissolved substances that move at different speeds on paper or a column.

qs.q: Cream is separated from milk by:
qs.e: Spinning milk fast throws the heavier part outward and lighter cream collects at the centre.

qs.q: The gases of air (nitrogen, oxygen, argon) are separated by:
qs.e: Air is liquefied and then warmed; gases boil off at different temperatures (nitrogen −196 °C, argon −186 °C, oxygen −183 °C).

qs.q: Petrol, diesel and kerosene are obtained from crude oil by:
qs.e: Crude oil (petroleum) is heated in a fractionating column and its fractions are drawn off by boiling range.

qs.q: Which of these is a colloid?
qs.e: Milk is an emulsion — fat droplets spread through water. Salt and sugar solutions are true solutions; muddy water is a suspension.

qs.q: The scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles is called the:
qs.e: Sunbeams in a dusty room or headlights in fog show the Tyndall effect.

qs.q: A mixture of oil and water can be separated using a:
qs.e: Oil and water do not mix; the heavier water is drained from the bottom of the funnel.

qs.q: Ammonium chloride can be separated from common salt by:
qs.e: On heating, ammonium chloride sublimes and can be collected; salt stays behind.

qs.q: Iron filings mixed with sulphur powder can be separated with a:
qs.e: Iron is magnetic, sulphur is not. If heated together they form iron sulphide, a compound that cannot be separated by a magnet.

qs.q: Alum is added to muddy water to:
o: Make the mud particles settle faster
qs.e: This is loading: alum makes fine particles clump together and settle.

qs.q: Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
qs.e: Sand and water can be seen separately and settle apart. The other three are uniform throughout.

qs.q: Fog is an example of a colloid in which:
o: A liquid is dispersed in a gas
A gas is dispersed in a liquid
A solid is dispersed in a gas
A solid is dispersed in a liquid
qs.e: Fog, mist and clouds are liquid-in-gas aerosols. Smoke is solid-in-gas.

qs.q: Which of these is an emulsion?
qs.e: An emulsion is a liquid dispersed in another liquid. Smoke is an aerosol, jelly a gel, pumice a solid foam.

qs.q: Particles in a true solution are smaller than about:
qs.e: True solution particles are below 1 nm; colloids are 1–1000 nm; suspensions larger.

qs.q: Pure crystals of copper sulphate are best obtained from its impure sample by:
qs.e: Crystallisation leaves soluble impurities in the solution; evaporating to dryness would leave them in the solid.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a mixture?
qs.e: Distilled water is pure H₂O, a compound. Soil, petrol and steel are mixtures.

qs.q: Approximately what percentage of air is nitrogen?
qs.e: Air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%.

qs.q: Blood is an example of a:
qs.e: Blood plasma carries proteins and cells in colloidal form; it shows the Tyndall effect.

qs.q: Which property does a compound have that a mixture does not?
o: A fixed ratio of its parts by mass
Its parts keep their own properties
It can be separated by physical methods
Its parts can be present in any amount
qs.e: A compound always has the same ratio (law of definite proportions); a mixture does not.

qs.q: Who discovered the electron?
qs.e: Thomson found the electron in 1897 using cathode rays.

qs.q: The neutron was discovered by:
qs.e: Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 and got the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935.

qs.q: Rutherford's gold foil (alpha particle scattering) experiment led to the discovery of the:
qs.e: Most alpha particles passed through but a few bounced back, showing a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus with mostly empty space around it.

qs.q: Which sub-atomic particle has no charge?
qs.e: Neutrons are neutral; protons are positive; electrons negative.

qs.q: The 'plum pudding' model of the atom was given by:
qs.e: Thomson pictured a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded like plums (or watermelon seeds).

qs.q: The idea that electrons revolve in fixed orbits (shells) without losing energy was given by:
qs.e: Bohr's model (1913) explained the stability of the atom and the line spectrum of hydrogen.

qs.q: The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of:
qs.e: Atomic number Z = protons (and = electrons in a neutral atom). It identifies the element.

qs.q: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is:
qs.e: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35 (this is chlorine-35).

qs.q: Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called:
qs.e: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons — e.g. C-12 and C-14.

qs.q: Argon-40 and calcium-40 are examples of:
qs.e: Isobars have the same mass number (40) but different atomic numbers (18 and 20).

qs.q: Which isotope of hydrogen is radioactive?
qs.e: Tritium (³H) has 1 proton and 2 neutrons and is radioactive. Protium and deuterium are stable.

qs.q: Which isotope is used to find the age of fossils?
qs.e: Radiocarbon dating uses carbon-14, with a half-life of about 5730 years.

qs.q: Cobalt-60 is used in:
qs.e: Gamma rays from cobalt-60 kill cancer cells (radiotherapy). Iodine-131 is used for the thyroid.

qs.q: The maximum number of electrons the M shell (n = 3) can hold is:
The electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11) is:
qs.e: K shell 2, L shell 8, M shell 1. The single outer electron makes sodium very reactive with valency 1.

qs.q: The valency of an element with electronic configuration 2, 8, 6 is:
qs.e: It needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet, so valency = 2. This is sulphur.

qs.q: The mass of an electron is about ______ of the mass of a proton.
qs.e: An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton.

qs.q: Canal rays (anode rays), which led to the discovery of the proton, were discovered by:
qs.e: Goldstein observed canal rays in 1886; the proton was later identified and named by Rutherford.

qs.q: The Indian sage who first said matter is made of tiny particles called 'parmanu' was:
qs.e: Kanad, founder of the Vaisheshika school, proposed the idea of parmanu long before Dalton.

qs.q: Carbon-14 and nitrogen-14 are examples of:
qs.e: Both have mass number 14 but atomic numbers 6 and 7.

qs.q: Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and F⁻ are isoelectronic because they all have:
qs.e: Each has 10 electrons — the same as neon.

qs.q: The principle that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers is:
qs.e: Pauli's exclusion principle limits each orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

qs.q: Which particle is found in the nucleus of every atom except ordinary hydrogen?
qs.e: Protium (¹H) has one proton and no neutron.

qs.q: Heavy water, used as a moderator in nuclear reactors, is:
qs.e: Heavy water is deuterium oxide, D₂O; it slows down neutrons.

qs.q: Who is known as the father of the periodic table?
qs.e: Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869 and left gaps for undiscovered elements.

qs.q: The modern periodic table is based on:
qs.e: Moseley showed in 1913 that properties repeat with atomic number — the modern periodic law.

qs.q: Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of increasing:
qs.e: Mendeleev's periodic law was based on atomic mass; Moseley later changed the basis to atomic number.

qs.q: The 'law of octaves' was given by:
qs.e: Newlands (1864) noticed every eighth element resembled the first, like notes of music.

qs.q: Döbereiner grouped elements in sets of:
qs.e: His triads (e.g. Li, Na, K) had the middle element's mass close to the average of the other two.

qs.q: How many periods are there in the modern periodic table?
How many groups are there in the modern periodic table?
Which is the most electronegative element?
qs.e: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (about 4.0 on the Pauling scale).

qs.q: On moving from left to right across a period, the atomic size:
qs.e: More protons pull the electrons in the same shell closer, so atoms get smaller.

qs.q: On moving down a group, metallic character:
qs.e: Larger atoms lose electrons more easily, so they are more metallic.

qs.q: Group 17 elements are called:
qs.e: Halogen means 'salt-former' — F, Cl, Br, I, At.

qs.q: Group 18 elements are known as:
qs.e: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon and oganesson have full outer shells and are very unreactive.

qs.q: Which of the following is an alkali metal?
qs.e: Group 1: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. Calcium and magnesium are alkaline earth metals.

qs.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
qs.e: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature; bromine is the liquid non-metal.

qs.q: Which non-metal is a liquid at room temperature?
qs.e: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Chlorine is a gas and iodine a solid.

qs.q: The most abundant element in the earth's crust is:
qs.e: Oxygen (about 46%), then silicon, then aluminium (the most abundant metal), then iron.

qs.q: The most abundant metal in the earth's crust is:
qs.e: Aluminium is about 8% of the crust, ahead of iron (about 5%).

qs.q: Elements in the same group have the same number of:
qs.e: That is why members of a group behave alike.

qs.q: Transition elements belong to the:
Lanthanides and actinides belong to the:
qs.e: They are the inner transition elements, placed in two rows at the bottom of the table.

qs.q: Which of the following is a metalloid?
qs.e: Metalloids — boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium — show properties of both metals and non-metals.

qs.q: The element with atomic number 1, placed in group 1 but a non-metal, is:
qs.e: Hydrogen has one electron like the alkali metals but is a non-metal gas.

qs.q: Which element has the highest melting point among metals and is used in bulb filaments?
qs.e: Tungsten melts at about 3422 °C. Nichrome is an alloy used in heater coils.

qs.q: Which metal can melt in the palm of your hand?
qs.e: Gallium melts at about 29.8 °C, below body temperature.

qs.q: The densest naturally occurring element is:
qs.e: Osmium (about 22.6 g/cm³) is slightly denser than iridium.

qs.q: Ionisation energy generally ______ down a group.
qs.e: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is easier to remove.

qs.q: Gallium and germanium were predicted by Mendeleev as:
qs.e: Their later discovery, matching his predictions, made his table famous.

qs.q: The number of elements in the modern periodic table is:
qs.e: 118 elements are known; the last four (113, 115, 117, 118) were named in 2016.

qs.q: Sodium chloride is formed by:
qs.e: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ held by electrostatic attraction.

qs.q: A covalent bond is formed by:
qs.e: Non-metal atoms share electron pairs to complete their octets.

qs.q: Which of these compounds is covalent?
qs.e: Methane is formed by sharing electrons between carbon and hydrogen; the others are ionic.

qs.q: The value of Avogadro's number is:
qs.e: One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

qs.q: The volume occupied by one mole of any gas at STP is:
qs.e: Molar volume at 0 °C and 1 atm is 22.4 litres.

qs.q: Ice floats on water because:
o: It is less dense than water due to hydrogen bonding
Water pushes it with an electric force
qs.e: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open cage in ice, so it is about 9% less dense than liquid water.

qs.q: Water has the maximum density at:
qs.e: This is why lakes freeze from the top and fish survive below.

qs.q: The unusually high boiling point of water is due to:
qs.e: Hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken before water can boil.

qs.q: How many moles are present in 88 g of carbon dioxide?
qs.e: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44 g; 88 ÷ 44 = 2 moles.

qs.q: The molar mass of water (H₂O) is:
The nitrogen molecule (N₂) has a:
qs.e: N≡N — the triple bond makes nitrogen very unreactive.

qs.q: Ionic compounds conduct electricity:
o: In molten state or in water solution
qs.e: Their ions are fixed in the solid crystal but free to move when melted or dissolved.

qs.q: Which law states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction?
qs.e: Given by Antoine Lavoisier, the father of modern chemistry.

qs.q: Who is called the father of modern chemistry?
qs.e: Lavoisier established conservation of mass and named oxygen and hydrogen.

qs.q: The law of definite (constant) proportions was given by:
qs.e: Proust: a compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass.

qs.q: The shape of the methane molecule is:
qs.e: Four C–H bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°.

qs.q: The shape of the carbon dioxide molecule is:
qs.e: O=C=O with a bond angle of 180°, so CO₂ is non-polar even though each bond is polar.

qs.q: The bond in which both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom is a:
qs.e: Also called a dative bond — e.g. in the ammonium ion NH₄⁺.

qs.q: The 'sea of electrons' model explains the bonding in:
qs.e: Free electrons let metals conduct electricity and heat.

qs.q: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of molecules. This is:
How many molecules are there in 18 g of water?
qs.e: 18 g of water is 1 mole, so it has Avogadro's number of molecules.

qs.q: Which of these is a polar molecule?
qs.e: Water is bent, so its bond polarities do not cancel. The others are non-polar.

qs.q: Graphite conducts electricity even though it is covalent because:
o: Each carbon has one free electron
qs.e: Each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one electron free to move between layers.

qs.q: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ is an example of a:
qs.e: Two substances combine to form one. It is also strongly exothermic.

qs.q: When an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution, the blue colour fades because:
o: Iron displaces copper from the solution
qs.e: Iron is more reactive than copper: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ (pale green) + Cu (brown coat on the nail).

qs.q: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl is a:
qs.e: Ions are exchanged and white insoluble barium sulphate precipitates.

qs.q: Which of the following is an endothermic process?
qs.e: Photosynthesis absorbs light energy. Respiration and burning release energy.

qs.q: Respiration is considered an exothermic reaction because:
o: Energy is released when glucose is oxidised

qs.q: Oxidation is:
o: Gain of oxygen or loss of electrons
qs.e: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); reduction is gain of electrons, gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.

qs.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, the substance oxidised is:
qs.e: Hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidised); copper oxide loses oxygen (reduced).

qs.q: Rust is chemically:
qs.e: Rust is Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, formed when iron meets both oxygen and moisture.

qs.q: Rusting of iron requires:
qs.e: Iron does not rust in dry air or in boiled (air-free) water.

qs.q: The process in which fats and oils are oxidised and develop a bad smell and taste is called:
qs.e: Rancidity is slowed by antioxidants, airtight containers, refrigeration and flushing with nitrogen.

qs.q: Chip packets are filled with which gas to prevent rancidity?
qs.e: Nitrogen is unreactive and pushes out oxygen, so the oil in chips does not oxidise.

qs.q: A substance that changes the rate of a reaction without itself being used up is a:
qs.e: Catalysts are recovered unchanged in mass and chemical make-up at the end.

qs.q: Biological catalysts are called:
qs.e: Enzymes such as amylase, pepsin and zymase speed up reactions in living things.

qs.q: Which catalyst is used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make vanaspati ghee?
qs.e: Hydrogen is added to unsaturated oils over nickel, turning them into solid fat.

qs.q: The decomposition of silver chloride in sunlight is used in:
qs.e: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ in light; silver bromide behaves the same way.

qs.q: Heating limestone (CaCO₃) to give quicklime and carbon dioxide is a:
When lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution, the precipitate formed is:
Copper vessels slowly develop a green coat because of the formation of:
qs.e: Copper reacts with moist CO₂ in air to form green basic copper carbonate.

qs.q: Silver articles turn black in air due to the formation of:
qs.e: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds (H₂S) in air to give black Ag₂S.

qs.q: Dissolving ammonium chloride in water makes the test tube feel:
qs.e: The process absorbs heat from the surroundings.

qs.q: In the balanced equation 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + xH₂, the value of x is:
qs.e: 8 hydrogen atoms on the left need 4 H₂ on the right.

qs.q: Whitewash turns shiny after a few days because slaked lime reacts with:
o: Carbon dioxide in air, forming calcium carbonate
qs.e: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O; the thin CaCO₃ layer gives the shine.

qs.q: Which change is a chemical change?
qs.e: Burning makes new substances (CO₂, water, ash). The others only change form or state.

qs.q: Which factor does NOT generally increase the rate of a reaction?
o: Using larger lumps of the reactant
qs.e: Larger lumps have less surface area, so the reaction is slower.

qs.q: Vinegar contains:
qs.e: Vinegar is about 5–8% acetic (ethanoic) acid in water.

qs.q: The acid present in lemon is:
qs.e: Citrus fruits contain citric acid along with ascorbic acid (vitamin C).

qs.q: Which acid is present in tamarind?
qs.e: Tamarind and grapes contain tartaric acid.

qs.q: The acid found in tomato is:
qs.e: Tomatoes and spinach contain oxalic acid (and some citric and malic acid).

qs.q: Curd is sour because it contains:
qs.e: Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid.

qs.q: An ant sting contains:
qs.e: Formic (methanoic) acid causes the pain; rubbing baking soda neutralises it.

qs.q: The acid in our stomach (gastric juice) is:
qs.e: HCl in the stomach kills germs and activates the enzyme pepsin.

qs.q: The pH of human blood is about:
qs.e: Blood is slightly basic, kept between 7.35 and 7.45.

qs.q: The pH scale was introduced by:
qs.e: Sørensen, a Danish chemist, introduced pH in 1909.

qs.q: A solution with pH 2 is:
qs.e: The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic. pH 2 is like lemon juice.

qs.q: A solution turns red litmus blue. Its pH is likely to be:
qs.e: Bases turn red litmus blue and have pH above 7.

qs.q: Phenolphthalein turns ______ in a basic solution.
qs.e: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and neutral solutions and pink in bases.

qs.q: Methyl orange shows which colour in an acidic solution?
qs.e: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.

qs.q: Turmeric turns reddish brown when it touches:
qs.e: A curry stain turns red when washed with soap because soap is basic.

qs.q: Litmus is obtained from:
qs.e: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens.

qs.q: Aqua regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and nitric acid in the ratio:
qs.e: Three parts HCl to one part HNO₃; it dissolves gold and platinum ('royal water').

qs.q: Which acid is called the 'king of chemicals'?
qs.e: Sulphuric acid is used in fertilisers, batteries, detergents, paints and refining — so widely that a country's use of it shows its industrial growth.

qs.q: Which of the following is used as an antacid?
qs.e: Milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) is a mild base that neutralises excess stomach acid.

qs.q: A bee sting is treated with baking soda because the sting is:
qs.e: The mild base neutralises the acid. A wasp sting is alkaline and is treated with vinegar.

qs.q: To treat acidic soil, farmers add:
qs.e: A base neutralises the extra acidity.

qs.q: While diluting a concentrated acid, one should:
o: Add acid slowly to water with stirring
qs.e: Mixing gives out a lot of heat; adding water to acid can make it boil and splash.

qs.q: When an acid reacts with a metal like zinc, the gas evolved is:
qs.e: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂; the gas burns with a pop sound.

qs.q: When an acid reacts with a carbonate, the gas released turns lime water milky. The gas is:
qs.e: CO₂ reacts with lime water to form insoluble calcium carbonate (milky).

qs.q: Tooth decay starts when the pH of the mouth falls below about:
qs.e: Bacteria make acid from sugar; toothpaste, being basic, neutralises it.

qs.q: The pH of pure water at 25 °C is:
Milk of magnesia is chemically:
Acid rain has a pH below:
qs.e: Normal rain is slightly acidic (about 5.6) from dissolved CO₂; acid rain is lower due to SO₂ and NO₂.

qs.q: Which of these is a strong acid?
qs.e: Strong acids ionise completely: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃.

qs.q: Soluble bases are called:
qs.e: NaOH, KOH and Ca(OH)₂ are alkalis. All alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkalis.

qs.q: Acid + base → salt + water. This reaction is called:
qs.e: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; the remaining ions form the salt.

qs.q: The acid found in apples is:
qs.e: Malic acid gives apples their sour taste.

qs.q: Tea contains:
qs.e: Tannins give tea its slightly bitter, astringent taste.

qs.q: An olfactory indicator changes its:
o: Smell in acidic or basic medium
qs.e: Onion, vanilla and clove oil are olfactory indicators — their smell disappears in a base.

qs.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
Sodium is stored in:
qs.e: Sodium reacts violently with water and oxygen, so it is kept under kerosene.

qs.q: White phosphorus is stored under:
qs.e: It catches fire in air at about 30 °C, so it is kept under water.

qs.q: The best conductor of electricity is:
qs.e: Silver conducts best; copper is used in wires because it is far cheaper.

qs.q: The most malleable metal is:
qs.e: Gold can be beaten into sheets thin enough for light to pass through; it is also the most ductile.

qs.q: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
qs.e: Graphite has free electrons between its layers.

qs.q: Which non-metal is lustrous (shiny)?
qs.e: Iodine crystals are shiny even though it is a non-metal.

qs.q: Galvanisation is the coating of iron with:
qs.e: Zinc protects iron even when the coating is scratched, because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first.

qs.q: Tin cans used to store food are made of iron coated with tin because tin is:
o: Less reactive than iron and non-toxic
qs.e: Tin forms a protective, non-poisonous layer; zinc would react with acids in food.

qs.q: Which metal does NOT liberate hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid?
qs.e: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.

qs.q: Which of these is the most reactive metal?
qs.e: Potassium is at the top of the reactivity series.

qs.q: Oxides of metals are generally:
qs.e: Metal oxides (Na₂O, MgO, CaO) form bases with water.

qs.q: Oxides of non-metals such as CO₂ and SO₂ are:
qs.e: They dissolve in water to give acids (carbonic, sulphurous acid). CO, NO and N₂O are neutral exceptions.

qs.q: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases is called:
qs.e: Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric.

qs.q: The thermite reaction (Fe₂O₃ + 2Al) is used for:
qs.e: Aluminium reduces iron oxide with so much heat that the iron comes out molten.

qs.q: Which metal can be cut with a knife?
qs.e: Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife.

qs.q: The hardest natural substance is:
qs.e: Diamond, an allotrope of carbon, is the hardest natural substance.

qs.q: The lightest metal is:
qs.e: Lithium has a density of about 0.53 g/cm³ — it floats on water.

qs.q: Aluminium utensils resist corrosion because:
o: A thin protective layer of aluminium oxide forms
Aluminium does not react with oxygen
qs.e: The oxide layer stops further reaction; anodising makes it thicker.

qs.q: Which of these is a noble metal?
qs.e: Gold, silver and platinum resist corrosion and oxidation.

qs.q: Which metal is used in the filaments of electric bulbs?
qs.e: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals (about 3422 °C).

qs.q: Metals are malleable and ductile because of:
qs.e: Layers of metal ions can slide over each other while the electron sea holds them together.

qs.q: The process of coating a thin layer of a metal over another using electricity is called:
qs.e: E.g. chromium plating on taps and cycle handles.

qs.q: Protecting a ship's iron hull by attaching blocks of magnesium or zinc is called:
qs.e: The more reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron.

qs.q: Which metal is a poor conductor of heat?
qs.e: Lead and mercury are relatively poor conductors of heat.

qs.q: Which of these reacts violently with cold water?
qs.e: Sodium reacts violently; magnesium reacts with hot water, iron with steam, copper not at all.

qs.q: The chemical formula of baking soda is:
qs.e: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate).
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: The chemical formula of washing soda is:
qs.e: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate — it has 10 molecules of water of crystallisation.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Bleaching powder is chemically:
qs.e: It is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Plaster of Paris is obtained by heating:
qs.e: Heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) at about 100 °C gives plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O).
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: The chemical formula of plaster of Paris is:
qs.e: Calcium sulphate hemihydrate — half a molecule of water per CaSO₄.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Gypsum is:
qs.e: Calcium sulphate dihydrate; it is added to cement to slow its setting.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Which compound is used to remove the permanent hardness of water?
qs.e: Sodium carbonate precipitates calcium and magnesium as insoluble carbonates.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Bleaching powder is used for:
qs.e: It releases chlorine, which kills germs; it is also used to bleach cotton and linen.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Baking powder is a mixture of baking soda and:
qs.e: Tartaric acid reacts with the sodium carbonate formed, so the cake does not taste bitter.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Blue vitriol is:
qs.e: CuSO₄·5H₂O — blue crystals; used as a fungicide (Bordeaux mixture).
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Green vitriol is:
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: White vitriol is:
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: 'Oil of vitriol' is the old name of:
qs.e: H₂SO₄ was once made by distilling green vitriol, hence the name.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Laughing gas is:
qs.e: N₂O causes mild euphoria and was used as an anaesthetic.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Marsh gas is:
qs.e: Methane bubbles up from marshes where plant matter rots without air.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: The indelible ink used in elections contains:
qs.e: Silver nitrate (lunar caustic) reacts with skin and darkens in light; it cannot be washed off for days.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Quicklime is:
qs.e: CaO; it reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Slaked lime is:
qs.e: Ca(OH)₂ — used for whitewashing; its clear solution is lime water.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Marble, limestone and chalk are all forms of:
qs.e: CaCO₃ — they differ in crystal structure and purity.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: The chemical name of caustic soda is:
qs.e: NaOH; used to make soap, paper and rayon.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Epsom salt is:
qs.e: MgSO₄·7H₂O, used as a laxative and in bath salts.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Glauber's salt is:
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Potash alum (phitkari) is used to:
o: Purify water and stop bleeding from small cuts
qs.e: Alum makes mud particles settle and is an astringent that stops minor bleeding.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Hypo, used in photography, is:
qs.e: Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O dissolves the unexposed silver bromide (fixing).
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Which gas is released at the anode during the electrolysis of brine (chlor-alkali process)?
qs.e: Chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide stays in the solution.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Sal ammoniac is:
qs.e: NH₄Cl, used in dry cells and in soldering flux.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Silver iodide is used for:
qs.e: AgI crystals help water vapour freeze into ice in clouds.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Saltpetre is:
qs.e: KNO₃ — a part of gunpowder (with charcoal and sulphur). Chile saltpetre is NaNO₃.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: When plaster of Paris is mixed with water, it sets into a hard mass of:
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Muriatic acid is the common name of:
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Which of the following is used in soda-acid fire extinguishers?
qs.e: Baking soda reacts with sulphuric acid to release CO₂, which smothers the fire.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: The number of water molecules in one formula unit of blue vitriol is:
qs.e: CuSO₄·5H₂O. Heating removes the water and leaves white anhydrous copper sulphate.
qs.tag: Common names and formulas of compounds

qs.q: Bauxite is an ore of:
qs.e: Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) is the main source of aluminium.

qs.q: Haematite is an ore of:
Galena is an ore of:
Cinnabar is an ore of:
Cassiterite (tinstone) is an ore of:
Zinc blende is:
Which is the richest ore of iron?
qs.e: Magnetite (Fe₃O₄) has about 72% iron. Haematite is mined more widely.

qs.q: Pitchblende is an ore of:
qs.e: Pitchblende (uraninite) is mainly uranium oxide; Marie Curie found radium and polonium in it.

qs.q: Monazite sand, found on the Kerala coast, is a source of:
qs.e: India has large reserves of thorium in monazite sands — the base of its three-stage nuclear programme.

qs.q: Froth flotation is used to concentrate:
qs.e: Sulphide particles stick to pine-oil froth and float off.

qs.q: Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air is called:
Heating a carbonate ore in limited or no air is called:
Aluminium is extracted from alumina by:
qs.e: Alumina dissolved in molten cryolite is electrolysed; aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon.

qs.q: In the blast furnace, limestone is added to:
qs.e: CaO from limestone combines with SiO₂ to form calcium silicate slag.

qs.q: Which is the purest form of iron?
qs.e: Wrought iron has the least carbon (below about 0.2%).

qs.q: Brass is an alloy of:
Bronze is an alloy of:
qs.e: Bronze = Cu + Sn; the Bronze Age is named after it.

qs.q: German silver contains:
qs.e: Despite the name it has no silver.

qs.q: Solder, used to join electric wires, is an alloy of:
qs.e: Solder has a low melting point.

qs.q: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with:
qs.e: Chromium forms a protective oxide layer, so stainless steel does not rust.

qs.q: Duralumin, used in aircraft, is mainly an alloy of:
o: Aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese

qs.q: Nichrome, used in heating elements, is an alloy of:
qs.e: It has high resistance and does not oxidise easily when red hot.

qs.q: An alloy of mercury with another metal is called:
qs.e: Silver-tin amalgam was widely used for dental fillings.

qs.q: 22-carat gold contains:
o: 22 parts gold and 2 parts copper or silver
qs.e: 24-carat gold is pure; 22 carat is about 91.6% gold, hardened for jewellery.

qs.q: Iron pyrites, called 'fool's gold', is:
qs.e: Its golden shine fooled miners, but it is iron disulphide.

qs.q: Invar, used in clock pendulums and measuring tapes, is an alloy of:
Alnico, used for making permanent magnets, contains:
Ultra-pure silicon for computer chips is obtained by:
qs.e: A molten zone carries the impurities to one end of the rod.

qs.q: Which metal is found in the free (native) state in nature?
qs.e: Unreactive metals like gold and platinum occur free.

qs.q: Cryolite is used in the extraction of aluminium because it:
o: Lowers the melting point of alumina and improves conductivity
Is an ore richer than bauxite
qs.e: Alumina melts above 2000 °C; dissolved in cryolite it can be electrolysed at about 950 °C.

qs.q: Pyrolusite is an ore of:
Which allotrope of carbon is a good conductor of electricity?
qs.e: Each carbon in graphite uses three electrons for bonding; the fourth is free to move.

qs.q: The hardest natural substance is an allotrope of:
qs.e: Diamond is pure carbon arranged in a rigid 3-D network.

qs.q: Buckminsterfullerene has the formula:
qs.e: 60 carbon atoms arranged like a football (pentagons and hexagons).

qs.q: Graphite is used as a lubricant because:
o: Its layers slide easily over one another
qs.e: Weak forces between layers let them slide.

qs.q: The ability of carbon to form long chains with itself is called:
qs.e: Catenation, together with valency 4, explains the huge number of carbon compounds.

qs.q: The general formula of alkanes is:
qs.e: Alkanes are saturated: only single bonds, e.g. CH₄, C₂H₆.

qs.q: The general formula of alkynes is:
qs.e: Alkynes have a triple bond, e.g. ethyne C₂H₂.

qs.q: Which gas is used for the artificial ripening of fruits?
qs.e: Ethylene (ethene) is a natural plant hormone that speeds ripening. Calcium carbide, which releases acetylene, is banned for this use.

qs.q: The gas used in oxy-acetylene welding is:
qs.e: Acetylene (ethyne) burns with oxygen at about 3000 °C.

qs.q: Formalin, used to preserve biological specimens, is an aqueous solution of:
qs.e: Formalin is about 40% formaldehyde (methanal) in water.

qs.q: Which compound is used as nail-polish remover?
qs.e: Acetone (propanone) is a ketone and a good solvent.

qs.q: Who first synthesised an organic compound (urea) in the laboratory?
qs.e: Wöhler made urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828, disproving the vital force theory.

qs.q: Consuming methanol (in spurious liquor) can cause:
qs.e: Methanol is oxidised in the body to formaldehyde and formic acid, which damage the optic nerve.

qs.q: Ethanol is commercially produced in India mainly by fermentation of:
qs.e: Yeast's enzymes convert the sugar in molasses (a by-product of sugar mills) into ethanol and CO₂.

qs.q: Ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding methanol and dyes is called:
qs.e: Denaturing prevents misuse of industrial alcohol.

qs.q: The functional group –COOH is present in:
Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures are called:
Two successive members of a homologous series differ by:
qs.e: They differ by a CH₂ unit, i.e. 14 u in mass.

qs.q: An acid reacts with an alcohol to form a sweet-smelling compound called an:
qs.e: Esterification — esters give fruity flavours and perfumes.

qs.q: The structure of benzene (a ring of six carbons) was proposed by:
qs.e: August Kekulé proposed the ring structure in 1865, reportedly after dreaming of a snake biting its own tail.

qs.q: Activated charcoal is used in gas masks and water filters because it:
o: Adsorbs gases and impurities on its large surface
Reacts with poisonous gases to give water

qs.q: Lampblack (soot) is used in making:
qs.e: It is an amorphous, very black form of carbon.

qs.q: Diamond sparkles mainly because of its:
o: High refractive index and total internal reflection
qs.e: With a refractive index of about 2.42, light is reflected many times inside a cut diamond.

qs.q: Graphene was isolated in 2004 by:
qs.e: They peeled it off graphite using sticky tape and won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

qs.q: Which is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
qs.e: Ethene has a C=C double bond; the others are alkanes with only single bonds.

qs.q: The monomer of PVC is:
Teflon, used to coat non-stick cookware, is a polymer of:
Polythene is a polymer of:
qs.e: Many ethene molecules join in addition polymerisation.

qs.q: The first fully synthetic fibre was:
qs.e: Nylon was made by Wallace Carothers at DuPont in 1935.

qs.q: Rayon is also called:
qs.e: Rayon is made from wood-pulp cellulose and looks like silk.

qs.q: Which fibre is known as artificial wool?
qs.e: Acrylic (polyacrylonitrile) is warm and cheap, used for sweaters and shawls.

qs.q: Thermocol is made of:
qs.e: Expanded polystyrene is light and a good insulator.

qs.q: Which of the following is a thermosetting plastic?
qs.e: Bakelite sets permanently on heating and cannot be remoulded.

qs.q: Melamine is used to make crockery because it is:
qs.e: Melamine resists heat and fire and does not soften.

qs.q: Bakelite is made from:
qs.e: Leo Baekeland made it in 1907 — the first fully synthetic plastic.

qs.q: Vulcanisation of rubber is done by heating it with:
qs.e: Sulphur cross-links rubber chains, making it harder and more elastic (Charles Goodyear).

qs.q: Natural rubber is a polymer of:
qs.e: cis-Polyisoprene from the latex of the rubber tree.

qs.q: Neoprene is a:
qs.e: Neoprene is polychloroprene, an oil-resistant synthetic rubber.

qs.q: Bullet-proof vests are made from:
qs.e: Kevlar, an aromatic polyamide, is five times stronger than steel by weight.

qs.q: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
qs.e: Cellulose (cotton, wood), starch, proteins and natural rubber are natural polymers.

qs.q: Rayon is a ______ fibre.
qs.e: It is regenerated from natural cellulose by chemical treatment.

qs.q: PET bottles are made of a type of:
Plastics that soften on heating and can be moulded again are called:
Nylon is used to make parachutes and climbing ropes because it is:
qs.e: A nylon thread is stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness.

qs.q: India banned many single-use plastic items from:
qs.e: The ban covers items like plastic cutlery, straws, earbuds with plastic sticks and thin carry bags.

qs.q: Which polymer is biodegradable?
qs.e: PHBV is broken down by bacteria; nylon-2-nylon-6 and PLA are also biodegradable.

qs.q: Latex from the rubber tree is coagulated using:
qs.e: The acid makes rubber particles clump together.

qs.q: Burning PVC is harmful mainly because it releases:
qs.e: Chlorine in PVC forms HCl gas and toxic dioxins on burning.

qs.q: Drugs that relieve pain are called:
qs.e: Aspirin, paracetamol and ibuprofen are analgesics.

qs.q: Drugs used to reduce fever are called:
Aspirin is chemically:
qs.e: Aspirin is an analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory drug; it also thins the blood.

qs.q: Penicillin was discovered by:
qs.e: Fleming noticed in 1928 that the mould Penicillium killed bacteria.

qs.q: Antibiotics are NOT effective against:
qs.e: Colds, flu and COVID-19 are viral; antibiotics act on bacteria.

qs.q: Dettol is a mixture of chloroxylenol and:
qs.e: Dettol is an antiseptic used on wounds and skin.

qs.q: Tincture of iodine is a/an:
qs.e: It is a 2–3% solution of iodine in alcohol and water, applied to wounds.

qs.q: Chemicals used to kill microorganisms on non-living objects such as floors are:
qs.e: Disinfectants (1% phenol, chlorine) are too harsh for skin.

qs.q: Which drug is used to treat malaria?
qs.e: Quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree; chloroquine and artemisinin are also used.

qs.q: Streptomycin is used to treat:
qs.e: Streptomycin was the first effective antibiotic against TB.

qs.q: Chloramphenicol is used to treat:
qs.e: It is a broad-spectrum antibiotic, notably against typhoid.

qs.q: Tranquillisers such as diazepam are used to:
qs.e: They act on the central nervous system.

qs.q: Cetirizine is an:
qs.e: Antihistamines control allergic reactions like sneezing and itching.

qs.q: Which artificial sweetener should NOT be used in cooking because it breaks down on heating?
qs.e: Aspartame is unstable at cooking temperatures; sucralose is heat-stable.

qs.q: Saccharin is about how many times sweeter than cane sugar?
qs.e: Saccharin is about 550 times sweeter and has no calories.

qs.q: Which chemical is commonly used to preserve fruit squashes and jams?
qs.e: Sodium benzoate stops the growth of yeasts, moulds and bacteria.

qs.q: Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is used in food as a:
BHA and BHT are added to foods as:
qs.e: They prevent fats from becoming rancid.

qs.q: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of:
qs.e: Made by saponification of oils or fats with an alkali.

qs.q: The process of making soap is called:
qs.e: Fat or oil + NaOH → soap + glycerol.

qs.q: Soaps do not lather well in hard water because:
o: They form insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium ions
qs.e: Detergents do not form scum, so they work in hard water.

qs.q: Which fertiliser has the highest nitrogen content?
Ammonia is manufactured by the:
qs.e: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ over an iron catalyst. The contact process makes H₂SO₄ and the Ostwald process HNO₃.

qs.q: Ordinary (soda-lime) glass is made from silica, sodium carbonate and:
qs.e: Sand + soda ash + limestone are melted together.

qs.q: Which glass is used for laboratory apparatus and ovenware because it expands very little on heating?
qs.e: Borosilicate glass resists sudden changes of temperature.

qs.q: Cobalt oxide gives glass a ______ colour.
qs.e: Chromium oxide gives green, manganese dioxide purple, cuprous oxide or gold ruby red.

qs.q: Glass is etched (engraved) using:
qs.e: HF reacts with silica in glass.

qs.q: Gypsum is added to cement to:
qs.e: Without gypsum, cement would set too quickly to be worked.

qs.q: Portland cement was invented by:
qs.e: Aspdin patented it in 1824; it looked like Portland stone when set.

qs.q: Dynamite was invented by:
qs.e: Nobel absorbed nitroglycerine in kieselguhr (1867); his fortune funds the Nobel Prizes.

qs.q: TNT, a well-known explosive, is:
qs.e: TNT is stable to handle and used in shells and mining.

qs.q: Gunpowder is a mixture of potassium nitrate, charcoal and:
qs.e: Black powder — the oldest known explosive.

qs.q: The side of a safety match box contains:
qs.e: The head (potassium chlorate + antimony trisulphide) ignites only when struck on this surface.

qs.q: The crimson red colour in fireworks is due to salts of:
qs.e: Barium gives green, sodium yellow, copper blue-green.

qs.q: Photochromic glass, which darkens in sunlight, contains:
qs.e: Light splits silver halide into dark silver; it reverses in the dark.

qs.q: Which of these is used as an antiseptic as well as a bleach for hair?
qs.e: H₂O₂ releases oxygen that kills germs and bleaches.

qs.q: Chloroform, once used as an anaesthetic, is stored in dark bottles because in light and air it forms:
qs.e: Chloroform oxidises in light to phosgene (COCl₂), a poison gas.

qs.q: LPG mainly contains:
qs.e: LPG is mainly butane with some propane, liquefied under pressure.

qs.q: The main component of CNG is:
qs.e: CNG is natural gas (mostly methane) compressed to about 200 bar.

qs.q: Biogas mainly consists of:
qs.e: Typically 50–75% methane, the rest mostly CO₂.

qs.q: Which compound is added to LPG to detect leaks by smell?
qs.e: Ethyl mercaptan (ethanethiol) has a strong rotten-cabbage smell.

qs.q: Which fuel has the highest calorific value?
qs.e: About 150,000 kJ/kg, but it is explosive and hard to store.

qs.q: The hottest part of a candle flame is the:
qs.e: Complete combustion happens in the outer zone; goldsmiths use it.

qs.q: The best quality coal with the highest carbon content is:
qs.e: Anthracite has about 90% or more carbon.

qs.q: Which type of coal has the lowest carbon content?
qs.e: Peat is the first stage of coal formation.

qs.q: Lignite is also called:
qs.e: Lignite is soft and brownish, between peat and bituminous coal.

qs.q: The octane number measures the quality of:
qs.e: Higher octane = less knocking. Cetane number rates diesel.

qs.q: The anti-knocking compound once added to petrol and now banned is:
qs.e: TEL caused lead pollution; India phased it out by 2000.

qs.q: Which fire extinguisher is most suitable for an electrical fire?
qs.e: CO₂ does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue.

qs.q: Water should NOT be used to put out a fire caused by burning oil because:
o: Oil floats on water and keeps burning, spreading the fire
qs.e: Use foam, sand or CO₂ instead.

qs.q: The minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire is called its:
qs.e: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and the ignition temperature.

qs.q: Burning of coal in a closed room is dangerous because it produces:
qs.e: CO combines with haemoglobin and stops oxygen transport.

qs.q: Water gas is a mixture of:
qs.e: Made by passing steam over red-hot coke.

qs.q: Producer gas is a mixture of:
qs.e: Made by passing air over red-hot coke.

qs.q: Petroleum is refined by:
qs.e: Its fractions are separated by their boiling ranges.

qs.q: Asia's oldest working oil refinery is at:
qs.e: Digboi in Assam started refining in 1901.

qs.q: Which of the following is obtained from the destructive distillation of coal?
o: Coke, coal tar and coal gas
qs.e: Heating coal without air gives coke, coal tar, coal gas and ammonia.

qs.q: Naphthalene balls are obtained from:
qs.e: Coal tar is a source of naphthalene, dyes, drugs and explosives.

qs.q: A fuel cell produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen, giving out:
qs.e: Fuel cells were used in the Apollo spacecraft and supply drinking water too.

qs.q: Which of these is an example of spontaneous combustion?
o: White phosphorus catching fire in air
qs.e: It catches fire on its own at about 30 °C.

qs.q: The fraction of petroleum with the highest boiling point among these is:
qs.e: Bitumen (asphalt) is the residue used for roads.

qs.q: At constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. This is:
qs.e: PV = constant at fixed temperature (Robert Boyle, 1662).

qs.q: At constant pressure, the volume of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. This is:
qs.e: V ∝ T, with T in kelvin.

qs.q: Soft drinks fizz when the bottle is opened because:
o: Pressure falls, so less CO₂ stays dissolved (Henry's law)
qs.e: Gas solubility is proportional to its pressure above the liquid.

qs.q: Fish find it hard to survive in warm water because:
o: Less oxygen dissolves in warm water
Fish cannot swim in warm water
qs.e: Gases are less soluble at higher temperatures.

qs.q: Raisins placed in water swell up due to:
qs.e: Water enters the raisin through its semi-permeable skin toward the more concentrated sugar solution.

qs.q: Water purifiers that remove dissolved salts by forcing water through a membrane work on:
qs.e: Pressure pushes water from the concentrated side to the dilute side, leaving salts behind.

qs.q: Water is called the universal solvent because:
o: It dissolves a very large number of substances
qs.e: Its polar molecules can surround and separate many kinds of ions and molecules.

qs.q: Which gas diffuses fastest?
qs.e: Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√(molar mass); hydrogen is the lightest.

qs.q: The ideal gas equation is:
qs.e: R is the universal gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K).

qs.q: The total pressure of a mixture of gases equals the sum of their partial pressures. This is:
Ethylene glycol is added to car radiators in cold countries because it:
o: Lowers the freezing point of water
qs.e: It acts as an anti-freeze — a colligative property.

qs.q: A solution in which no more solute can dissolve at a given temperature is:
qs.e: Adding more solute to a saturated solution leaves it undissolved.

qs.q: Pickles and jams do not spoil easily because the high salt or sugar:
o: Draws water out of microbes by osmosis
qs.e: Microbes lose water and cannot grow.

qs.q: Standard temperature and pressure (STP) means:
A tyre may burst on a hot summer day because:
o: Pressure of the air inside rises with temperature
The air inside turns into liquid
qs.e: At constant volume, pressure increases with temperature (Gay-Lussac's law).

qs.q: Deep-sea divers suffer 'the bends' when they surface quickly because:
o: Nitrogen dissolved in the blood under pressure forms bubbles
Carbon dioxide stops dissolving in blood
qs.e: Henry's law; helium–oxygen mixtures reduce this risk.

qs.q: The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was caused by the leakage of:
qs.e: MIC leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant on the night of 2–3 December 1984.

qs.q: The ozone layer is mainly damaged by:
qs.e: Chlorine atoms released from CFCs in sunlight destroy ozone molecules.

qs.q: The ozone layer is found in the:
The international treaty to protect the ozone layer is the:
qs.e: Signed in 1987 to phase out ozone-depleting substances.

qs.q: Which of these is the main greenhouse gas from human activity?
qs.e: CO₂ from burning fossil fuels contributes most to global warming.

qs.q: Acid rain is mainly caused by:
qs.e: They form sulphuric and nitric acids in clouds.

qs.q: The 'marble cancer' of the Taj Mahal is caused by:
qs.e: Acid rain reacts with calcium carbonate in marble; emissions from the Mathura refinery were blamed.

qs.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning with:
qs.e: Methyl mercury in fish at Minamata Bay, Japan.

qs.q: Itai-itai disease is caused by:
qs.e: Cadmium makes bones brittle and painful; 'itai' means 'it hurts' in Japanese.

qs.q: Blue baby syndrome is caused by excess ______ in drinking water.
qs.e: Nitrates reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen (methaemoglobinaemia).

qs.q: Black foot disease is associated with:
qs.e: Long-term arsenic in groundwater damages blood vessels in the feet.

qs.q: Excess fluoride in drinking water causes:
qs.e: Mottled teeth and stiff, deformed bones.

qs.q: Photochemical smog contains mainly:
qs.e: It forms in sunlight from vehicle exhaust (Los Angeles smog) and is oxidising.

qs.q: Classical (London) smog is a mixture of smoke, fog and:
qs.e: It is a reducing smog of cool, damp weather.

qs.q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it:
o: Combines with haemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport
qs.e: It binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen.

qs.q: Ozone depletion is measured in:
qs.e: One Dobson unit is a very thin layer of ozone at STP.

qs.q: World Ozone Day is observed on:
qs.e: Marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol in 1987.

qs.q: The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol aims to phase down:
qs.e: HFCs replaced CFCs but are powerful greenhouse gases.

qs.q: Excessive growth of algae in water bodies due to phosphates and nitrates is called:
qs.e: Algae use up oxygen when they decay, killing fish.

qs.q: A high BOD (biological oxygen demand) in a river indicates that the water is:
qs.e: Microbes need a lot of oxygen to break down the organic waste.

qs.q: A catalytic converter in a vehicle converts:
o: CO and nitrogen oxides into CO₂ and N₂
qs.e: Platinum, palladium and rhodium act as catalysts.

qs.q: Ozone at ground level is:
qs.e: High up it protects us from UV; near the ground it harms lungs and crops.

qs.q: Which gas is released from rice paddies and cattle and is a strong greenhouse gas?
qs.e: Methane traps much more heat per molecule than CO₂.

qs.q: Hydrogen was discovered by:
qs.e: Cavendish called it 'inflammable air' (1766); Lavoisier named it hydrogen.

qs.q: Oxygen was discovered independently by Scheele and:
qs.e: Priestley published in 1774; Lavoisier named it oxygen.

qs.q: Nitrogen was discovered by:
qs.e: Daniel Rutherford in 1772 — not Ernest Rutherford of the atomic nucleus.

qs.q: Which gas is filled in electric bulbs?
qs.e: Inert argon stops the hot tungsten filament from burning.

qs.q: Which gas is used in advertisement signs for its red-orange glow?
qs.e: Neon glows red-orange in a discharge tube.

qs.q: Helium is used in balloons and airships because it is:
qs.e: Hydrogen is lighter but catches fire — remember the Hindenburg disaster.

qs.q: Deep-sea divers breathe a mixture of oxygen and:
qs.e: Helium is less soluble in blood than nitrogen, reducing the bends.

qs.q: Which noble gas is radioactive?
qs.e: Radon comes from the decay of radium and uranium in rocks.

qs.q: The noble gases were discovered mainly by:
qs.e: Ramsay (with Lord Rayleigh for argon) won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1904.

qs.q: Temporary hardness of water is due to the presence of:
qs.e: Boiling turns bicarbonates into insoluble carbonates.

qs.q: Permanent hardness of water is due to:
o: Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium
qs.e: These are not removed by boiling.

qs.q: Temporary hardness of water can be removed by:
qs.e: Also by Clark's method (adding slaked lime).

qs.q: Which of the following removes permanent hardness of water?
qs.e: Washing soda precipitates calcium and magnesium as carbonates; ion exchange and Calgon also work.

qs.q: Calgon, used to soften water, is:
qs.e: It traps Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in soluble complexes.

qs.q: Deuterium was discovered by:
qs.e: Urey won the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

qs.q: Which gas turns lime water milky?
Carbon dioxide was first identified as 'fixed air' by:
Chlorine gas was discovered by:
qs.e: Scheele in 1774; Davy proved it was an element.

qs.q: Which gas smells like rotten eggs?
qs.e: H₂S is poisonous even in small amounts.

qs.q: Liquid nitrogen, used to preserve biological samples, boils at about:

qs.e: Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921; R. D. Banerji found Mohenjodaro in 1922. John Marshall then headed the ASI.

qs.q: The Great Bath is located at:
qs.e: The Great Bath, about 11.88 m by 7.01 m and 2.43 m deep, is the most famous structure of Mohenjodaro.

qs.q: The only Harappan site with a dockyard is:
qs.e: Lothal in Gujarat has the dockyard and is called the 'Manchester of the Indus'.

qs.q: The earliest evidence of a ploughed field in the Indian subcontinent was found at:
qs.e: Kalibangan in Rajasthan, on the Ghaggar, gave the earliest ploughed field; Banawali gave a toy plough.

qs.q: The largest Harappan site in India is:
qs.e: Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is the largest Harappan site in India; Mohenjodaro, the largest overall, is in Pakistan.

qs.q: Harappan bricks were made in the ratio:
qs.e: Burnt bricks of the ratio 4:2:1 (length : breadth : thickness), laid in English bond, are a Harappan signature.

qs.q: Dholavira is famous for its:
qs.e: Dholavira (Gujarat) has elaborate water reservoirs, a stadium and a three-part town plan; it is a UNESCO site.

qs.q: Which metal was NOT known to the Harappans?
qs.e: The Harappan civilisation belongs to the Bronze Age; iron was unknown to it.

qs.q: The southernmost site of the Indus Valley Civilisation is:
qs.e: Corners MAD-S: Manda north, Alamgirpur east, Daimabad south, Sutkagendor west.

qs.q: Horse bones were found at which Harappan site?
qs.e: Surkotada in Gujarat gave the first clear horse bones — but no horse appears on any Harappan seal.

qs.q: Chanhudaro is best known as a centre of:
qs.e: Chanhudaro was a bead-making centre, and the only major Harappan site without a citadel.

qs.q: The Harappan script is described as 'boustrophedon', which means it was written:
o: Right to left and then left to right in alternate lines
qs.e: Boustrophedon writing turns at the end of each line, like a plough. The script is still undeciphered.

qs.q: Harappan weights were generally in multiples of:
qs.e: Harappan weights followed a binary then decimal scheme, with 16 and its multiples prominent.

qs.q: The easternmost site of the Harappan civilisation is:
qs.e: Alamgirpur on the Hindon in Uttar Pradesh is the easternmost Harappan site.

qs.q: Which animal is most commonly shown on Harappan seals?
qs.e: The humped bull and the 'unicorn' dominate the seals. The horse and lion are absent.

qs.q: Which of these was NOT found in any Harappan city?
qs.e: No structure has been identified as a temple anywhere in the Harappan world.

qs.q: Mohenjodaro literally means:
qs.e: Mohenjodaro, on the Indus in Sindh, means 'mound of the dead' in Sindhi.

qs.q: The Gayatri Mantra is found in which Mandala of the Rigveda?
qs.e: The Gayatri Mantra, addressed to Savitri, is in Mandala III of the Rigveda.

qs.q: 'Satyameva Jayate', India's national motto, is taken from:
qs.e: It comes from the Mundaka Upanishad, part of the Atharvaveda tradition.

qs.q: Which Veda is considered the root of Indian music?
qs.e: The Samaveda sets the hymns to melody, so Indian classical music traces itself to it. Trick: Sama → Sangeet.

qs.q: The priest associated with the Yajurveda is the:
qs.e: Priests in Veda order R-Y-S-A are Hotri, Adhvaryu, Udgatri, Brahma (HAUB).

qs.q: The Purusha Sukta, which describes the origin of the four varnas, occurs in:
qs.e: The Purusha Sukta and the Nadi Sukta both appear in the tenth and latest Mandala of the Rigveda.

qs.q: The Vedic name of the river Sutlej is:
qs.e: West to east the Punjab rivers are Vitasta (Jhelum), Askini (Chenab), Parushni (Ravi), Vipasha (Beas), Shutudri (Sutlej).

qs.q: Which river is mentioned most often in the Rigveda?
qs.e: The Sindhu (Indus) is the most frequently mentioned; the Saraswati is called the holiest (Naditama).

qs.q: How many hymns does the Rigveda contain?
qs.e: The Rigveda has 1,028 hymns (suktas) arranged in 10 mandalas.

qs.q: The chief deity of the Rigveda, with about 250 hymns to his name, is:
qs.e: Indra comes first with roughly 250 hymns, followed by Agni with about 200. Prajapati rises only in the Later Vedic age.

qs.q: Which Vedic assembly is believed to be the oldest, and the only one in which women took part?
qs.e: The Vidatha was the oldest assembly; it disappeared in the Later Vedic period.

qs.q: Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gandharvaveda and Shilpaveda are known as:
qs.e: These four are the Upavedas. The six Vedangas are Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chhanda and Jyotisha.

qs.q: The Atharvaveda mainly deals with:
qs.e: The Atharvaveda collects charms, spells and cures, which is why it is also called the Brahmaveda.

qs.q: The Nyaya school of Indian philosophy was founded by:
qs.e: Samkhya–Kapila, Yoga–Patanjali, Nyaya–Gautama, Vaisheshika–Kanada, Mimamsa–Jaimini, Vedanta–Badarayana.

qs.q: Which pottery type is associated with the Later Vedic period?
qs.e: Painted Grey Ware marks the Later Vedic period in the Ganga–Yamuna doab; NBP Ware comes after it.

qs.q: How many principal Upanishads are there, out of 108 in all?
qs.e: Of the 108 Upanishads, 13 are regarded as principal.

qs.q: Which of these was NOT a feature of the Later Vedic period?
o: Cattle rearing as the main source of wealth
Large sacrifices such as the Rajasuya
The rise of Prajapati as the chief god
qs.e: Cattle wealth and pastoralism belong to the Early (Rig) Vedic period; the Later Vedic economy was agricultural.

qs.q: Gautama Buddha delivered his first sermon at:
qs.e: Enlightenment came at Bodh Gaya, but the first sermon (Dharmachakra Pravartana) was at Sarnath's Deer Park.

qs.q: Gautama Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana at:
qs.e: He died at Kushinagar (UP) at the age of 80.

qs.q: Mahavira was the:
qs.e: Jainism was not founded by Mahavira; he was the 24th and last Tirthankara, and a reformer.

qs.q: The symbol of Mahavira as a Tirthankara is the:
qs.e: Rishabhanatha's symbol is the bull, Parshvanatha's the snake, Neminatha's the conch and Mahavira's the lion.

qs.q: The Fourth Buddhist Council was held under the patronage of:
qs.e: Councils Ra-Vai-Pa-Ka were held under Ajatashatru, Kalashoka, Ashoka and Kanishka respectively.

qs.q: The Third Buddhist Council was presided over by:
qs.e: It met at Pataliputra under Ashoka, and added the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

qs.q: Which of the Three Pitakas deals with monastic discipline?
qs.e: Vinaya = rules of the Sangha, Sutta = the Buddha's discourses, Abhidhamma = philosophy.

qs.q: In Buddhist art, the horse is a symbol of Buddha's:
qs.e: Lotus/bull = birth, horse = renunciation, bodhi tree = enlightenment, wheel = first sermon, stupa = death.

qs.q: Which text lists the sixteen Mahajanapadas?
qs.e: The Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya names the sixteen Mahajanapadas; the Jain Bhagavati Sutra also lists them.

qs.q: Which Mahajanapada was a republic (gana-sangha) with its capital at Vaishali?
qs.e: Vajji and Malla were the two republics; the rest were monarchies.

qs.q: Who shifted the Magadhan capital from Rajgriha to Pataliputra?
qs.e: Ajatashatru fortified Pataliputra; his successor Udayin made it the capital.

qs.q: The fifth vow of Brahmacharya was added to Jainism by:
qs.e: Parshvanatha had taught four vows; Mahavira added Brahmacharya (celibacy) as the fifth.

qs.q: The Jain doctrine that truth has many sides is called:
qs.e: Syadvada or Anekantavada is the Jain theory of the many-sidedness of reality.

qs.q: The Ajivika sect was founded by:
qs.e: Makkhali Gosala's Ajivika sect taught strict fatalism (niyati).

qs.q: Mahavira was born at:
qs.e: He was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali and died at Pavapuri in Bihar.

qs.q: The language used by Mahavira to preach was:
qs.e: Mahavira preached in Prakrit (Ardha-Magadhi); the Buddha used Pali.

qs.q: Which dynasty of Magadha was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya?
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya, helped by Chanakya, defeated the last Nanda ruler Dhanananda.

qs.q: The Kalinga war was fought in:
qs.e: Ashoka fought Kalinga in 261 BCE and described his remorse in Rock Edict XIII.

qs.q: In which of his edicts does Ashoka describe the Kalinga war?
qs.e: Rock Edict XIII is the longest and records the Kalinga war; Edict XII deals with religious tolerance.

qs.q: The Brahmi script of Ashoka's edicts was deciphered in 1837 by:
qs.e: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, unlocking the Ashokan inscriptions.

qs.q: Ashoka's personal name appears in which of his inscriptions?
o: The Maski and Gujarra minor rock edicts
qs.e: Elsewhere he is 'Devanampiya Piyadassi'; only Maski, Gujarra, Nittur and Udegolam use the name Ashoka.

qs.q: The Mauryan official in charge of state agriculture was the:
qs.e: Sita = crown land, so Sitadhyaksha looked after state agriculture; Panyadhyaksha handled commerce.

qs.q: Who was the Mauryan official in charge of tolls and customs?
qs.e: Sulka = toll. Pautava = weights and measures, Samstha = markets, Nava = shipping.

qs.q: Chandragupta Maurya spent his last days as a follower of:
qs.e: He abdicated, became a Jain under Bhadrabahu and died by sallekhana at Shravanabelagola.

qs.q: Megasthenes was the ambassador of which ruler at the Mauryan court?
qs.e: Seleucus sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta Maurya after the treaty of 305 BCE.

qs.q: The National Emblem of India is taken from the Lion Capital at:
qs.e: The Sarnath Lion Capital was adopted as the National Emblem on 26 January 1950.

qs.q: The new post created by Ashoka to propagate dhamma was the:
qs.e: Dhamma Mahamattas were officers appointed specially to spread and supervise dhamma.

qs.q: The last ruler of the Mauryan dynasty was:
qs.e: Brihadratha was killed in about 185 BCE by his general Pushyamitra Sunga.

qs.q: The chief revenue collector in the Mauryan administration was the:
qs.e: Samaharta collected revenue; Sannidhata was the treasurer.

qs.q: Mauryan coins were mainly:
qs.e: Punch-marked silver coins, called pana or karshapana, were the standard Mauryan currency.

qs.q: Which Ashokan inscription records his visit to the Buddha's birthplace?
qs.e: The Rummindei pillar records the visit and the tax relief he granted the village.

qs.q: Megasthenes recorded that Indian society was divided into how many classes?
qs.e: Megasthenes spoke of seven castes, not the four varnas, and said there was no slavery in India.

qs.q: Ashoka's edicts in the north-west were written in which script?
qs.e: Kharosthi was used at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra; Greek and Aramaic appear at Kandahar.

qs.q: Which Mauryan ruler bore the title 'Amitraghata'?
qs.e: Bindusara, Ashoka's father, was called Amitraghata — 'slayer of foes'.

qs.q: The Saka era, used as India's national calendar, was started in 78 CE by:
qs.e: Kanishka began the Saka era in 78 CE; it was adopted as India's national calendar on 22 March 1957.

qs.q: The Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription, the first long inscription in Sanskrit, belongs to:
qs.e: Rudradaman I, a Shaka ruler, recorded the repair of the Sudarshana lake in it.

qs.q: The Hathigumpha inscription is associated with:
qs.e: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is at Udayagiri in Odisha; he was a Jain.

qs.q: Which dynasty was the first in India to issue lead coins?
qs.e: The Satavahanas issued lead coins; the Indo-Greeks issued the first gold coins and the Kushanas the purest.

qs.q: The Gandhara school of art was strongly influenced by:
qs.e: Gandhara sculpture shows Greek influence — wavy hair, muscular bodies and folded drapery in grey schist.

qs.q: The Mathura school of sculpture mainly used:
qs.e: Mathura used spotted red sandstone; Gandhara used grey schist and Amaravati white marble.

qs.q: The capital of the Satavahanas was:
qs.e: Pratishthana, modern Paithan in Maharashtra, was the Satavahana capital.

qs.q: The Greek ruler Menander, who became a Buddhist, features in which text?
qs.e: Milindapanho ('Questions of Milinda') records his dialogue with the monk Nagasena.

qs.q: Kanishka's capital was:
qs.e: Purushapura, modern Peshawar, was Kanishka's capital; Mathura was a second centre.

qs.q: The oldest extant work of Tamil literature is:
qs.e: Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar is a work on Tamil grammar and poetics, the oldest Tamil text.

qs.q: The Thirukkural, often called the 'Tamil Veda', was composed by:
qs.e: Thiruvalluvar's Kural has 1,330 couplets on ethics and statecraft.

qs.q: The Chera capital during the Sangam Age was:
qs.e: Chera–Vanji, Chola–Uraiyur, Pandya–Madurai. Muziris was the Chera port.

qs.q: The Sunga dynasty was founded by:
qs.e: Pushyamitra Sunga founded the dynasty after killing the last Maurya, Brihadratha.

qs.q: The railings and gateways of the Sanchi stupa were added by the:
qs.e: Ashoka began the stupa; the Sungas and Satavahanas added the railings and the carved toranas.

qs.q: Which Satavahana ruler is regarded as the greatest of the line?
qs.e: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Shakas and is praised in the Nasik inscription of his mother Gautami Balashri.

qs.q: The Amaravati school of art chiefly used:
qs.e: Amaravati, in Andhra under the Satavahanas, worked in white marble with narrative panels.

qs.q: The Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayag Prashasti) praises:
qs.e: It was composed by Samudragupta's court poet Harisena and engraved on an Ashokan pillar.

qs.q: Samudragupta has been called the 'Indian Napoleon' by:
qs.e: The historian V. A. Smith gave him that name for his many conquests.

qs.q: The Gupta era began in:
qs.e: Chandragupta I started the Gupta era in 319–20 CE; the Saka era is 78 CE and the Vikrama Samvat 58 BCE.

qs.q: Nalanda University was founded by:
qs.e: Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda; Harsha only patronised it later and Dharmapala founded Vikramashila.

qs.q: Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of:
qs.e: Fa-Hien came in Chandragupta II's time and wrote Fo-Kuo-Ki; Hiuen Tsang came under Harsha.

qs.q: Which Gupta ruler took the title 'Shakari' after defeating the Shakas?
qs.e: Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' destroyed the Western Kshatrapas and took the title Shakari.

qs.q: Aryabhata's major astronomical work is:
qs.e: Aryabhatiya and Surya Siddhanta are Aryabhata's; Brihat Samhita is Varahamihira's.

qs.q: Who stated that the earth rotates on its axis and explained eclipses scientifically?
qs.e: Aryabhata said the earth is round and rotates, and explained solar and lunar eclipses.

qs.q: The Sushruta Samhita deals mainly with:
qs.e: Sushruta is called the father of plastic surgery; Charaka's Samhita deals with general medicine.

qs.q: Kalidasa's play about Shakuntala is called:
qs.e: Abhijnanashakuntalam is his best-known play; Meghaduta is a poem.

qs.q: Gupta gold coins were known as:
qs.e: The Guptas issued gold dinaras — the largest number of gold coins in ancient India.

qs.q: Which Gupta ruler repelled the Huna invasion?
qs.e: Skandagupta defeated the Hunas and also repaired the Sudarshana lake, as his Junagadh inscription records.

qs.q: The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh belongs to which period?
qs.e: It is a Gupta-period temple, one of the earliest examples of the Nagara style.

qs.q: Which Gupta ruler issued the famous 'Lyrist' (veena-playing) coin?
qs.e: Samudragupta's lyrist type shows him playing the veena, pointing to his love of music.

qs.q: Who was the court poet who composed the Allahabad Prashasti?
qs.e: Harisena served Samudragupta; Ravikirti wrote the Aihole inscription for Pulakeshin II.

qs.q: Chandragupta I married a princess of which clan, strengthening his position?
qs.e: His marriage to the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi is commemorated on his coins.

qs.q: Harshavardhana was defeated on the Narmada by:
qs.e: The Aihole inscription of Ravikirti records Pulakeshin II's victory over Harsha.

qs.q: The biography of Harshavardhana, the Harshacharita, was written by:
qs.e: Banabhatta, Harsha's court poet, also wrote Kadambari.

qs.q: The rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora was built by:
qs.e: Krishna I had it carved out of a single rock from the top down.

qs.q: The Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur was built by:
qs.e: Rajaraja I built it; it is one of the Great Living Chola Temples, a UNESCO site.

qs.q: The Khajuraho temples were built by the:
qs.e: Khajuraho, including the Kandariya Mahadeva temple, is Chandela work.

qs.q: The Konark Sun temple was built by:
o: Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Gangas
qs.e: Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty built it in the 13th century.

qs.q: The Dilwara Jain temples at Mount Abu were built under the:
qs.e: They belong to the Solanki period, which also produced the Modhera Sun temple and Rani ki Vav.

qs.q: Vikramashila University was founded by:
qs.e: Dharmapala of the Pala dynasty founded Vikramashila in Bihar.

qs.q: The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang's account of India is called:
qs.e: Si-Yu-Ki means 'Records of the Western World'. Fo-Kuo-Ki is Fa-Hien's.

qs.q: The Uttaramerur inscription is an important source on:
qs.e: It records how village assemblies were elected under the Cholas.

qs.q: Harshavardhana belonged to which dynasty?
qs.e: He belonged to the Pushyabhuti or Vardhana dynasty and ruled from Kannauj.

qs.q: The Shore temple and the rathas at Mahabalipuram were built by the:
qs.e: Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' gave Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) its name and monuments.

qs.q: The tripartite struggle for Kannauj was fought among the:
qs.e: The three powers fought over Kannauj through the 8th and 9th centuries.

qs.q: Amoghavarsha, who wrote Kavirajamarga in Kannada, belonged to which dynasty?
qs.e: Amoghavarsha I was a Rashtrakuta ruler and a patron of Kannada literature.

qs.q: The bronze Nataraja image is the finest achievement of which dynasty's art?
qs.e: Chola bronzes, cast by the lost-wax method, are famous above all for the dancing Shiva.

qs.q: Which ancient university was destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji in 1193?
qs.e: Nalanda was sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

qs.q: 'Mudrarakshasa', a play on the rise of Chandragupta Maurya, was written by:
qs.e: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa. Kalhana wrote Rajatarangini and Banabhatta the Harshacharita.

qs.q: The Sanskrit grammar 'Ashtadhyayi' was composed by:
qs.e: Panini's Ashtadhyayi is the oldest surviving Sanskrit grammar; Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya, a commentary on it.

qs.q: Neolithic ash mounds have been found mainly in:
qs.e: Sanganakallu and Piklihal in Karnataka are the famous ash-mound sites. Kashmir (Burzahom) is known for pit dwellings instead.

qs.q: The rock paintings of Bhimbetka were brought to light in 1957 by:
qs.e: Wakankar discovered the Bhimbetka shelters in 1957. Bruce Foote had found India's first Palaeolithic tool at Pallavaram in 1863.

qs.q: The 'Mahabhashya', a commentary on Panini's grammar, was written by:
qs.e: Patanjali's Mahabhashya explains the Ashtadhyayi and is also a source for Sunga-period history.

qs.q: The first metal to be used by human beings was:
qs.e: Copper came first, which is why the Stone-Copper phase is called Chalcolithic; iron appears much later, in the Later Vedic age.

qs.q: The bronze statuette known as the 'Dancing Girl' was found at:
qs.e: The Dancing Girl, cast by the lost-wax method, comes from Mohenjodaro, along with the bearded priest figure.

qs.q: Which Harappan site was the first to be excavated after Independence?
qs.e: Ropar (Rupnagar) on the Sutlej was taken up first after 1947; it also gave a dog buried with a human.

qs.q: The mature phase of the Harappan civilisation is dated to:
qs.e: The mature or urban phase ran from about 2600 to 1900 BCE; decline set in around 1900 BCE.

qs.q: Harappan seals were most commonly made of:
qs.e: Steatite (soft soapstone) was the usual material, cut square with an animal figure and a line of script.

qs.q: The Greeks called the cotton grown in the Indus region:
qs.e: Cotton was first cultivated by the Harappans, and the Greeks named it Sindon after the Sindhu (Indus).

qs.q: Coffin burial and the R-37 cemetery are associated with which Harappan site?
qs.e: Harappa gave the coffin burial and cemetery R-37; Lothal is famous for a double burial instead.

qs.q: A bronze chariot was among the finds at which Harappan site?
qs.e: Daimabad in Maharashtra, the southernmost Harappan site, gave the well-known bronze chariot and animal figures.

qs.q: Which Mandala of the Rigveda is devoted entirely to the god Soma?
qs.e: Mandala IX is the Soma Mandala. Mandala III has the Gayatri Mantra and Mandala X the Purusha Sukta.

qs.q: The Mahabharata, the longest poem in the world, is attributed to:
qs.e: Ved Vyasa composed the Mahabharata; Valmiki composed the Ramayana.

qs.q: Which scholar held that the original home of the Aryans was the Arctic region?
qs.e: Tilak argued for an Arctic home. Max Muller said Central Asia, Dayanand said Tibet and A. C. Das the Sapta-Sindhu itself.

qs.q: Which Veda has two recensions known as Shukla and Krishna?
qs.e: The Yajurveda, the book of sacrificial ritual, survives in a White (Shukla) and a Black (Krishna) recension.

qs.q: The prayer 'Asato Ma Sadgamaya' is taken from the:
qs.e: It comes from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. 'Satyameva Jayate' is from the Mundaka and 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' from the Maha Upanishad.

qs.q: The First Buddhist Council was held at:
qs.e: It met in the Sattapanni cave at Rajgriha under Ajatashatru, and compiled the Vinaya and Sutta Pitakas.

qs.q: Gautama Buddha attained enlightenment at the age of:
qs.e: He renounced the world at 29, gained enlightenment at 35 at Bodh Gaya, and died at 80 at Kushinagar.

qs.q: The Jain Agamas were finally written down at the second Jain council held at:
qs.e: The Valabhi council of 512 CE, under Devardhi Kshamasramana, put the Agamas in writing; the first council at Pataliputra had led to the Digambara-Svetambara split.

qs.q: The first woman to be admitted into the Buddhist Sangha was:
qs.e: Buddha's aunt and foster-mother Mahaprajapati Gotami was admitted on Ananda's pleading.

qs.q: The Charvaka or Lokayata school of materialism is traditionally attributed to:
qs.e: Brihaspati is named as the founder of Charvaka materialism. Makkhali Gosala founded the fatalist Ajivika sect.

qs.q: Which of these was NOT one of the four Mahajanapadas that fought for supremacy in north India?
qs.e: The four contenders were Magadha, Kosala, Avanti and Vatsa. Vajji was a republic, not one of the four monarchies in that struggle.

qs.q: Which of these was NOT a provincial capital of the Mauryan empire?
qs.e: The provincial capitals were Taxila, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Tosali, with Pataliputra as the imperial capital.

qs.q: A Mauryan provincial governor, usually a prince of the royal house, was called:
qs.e: The Kumara or Aryaputra headed a province. Rajjukas measured land and Pradeshikas were district officers.

qs.q: The queen named in Ashoka's so-called 'Queen's Edict' is:
qs.e: The edict mentions queen Karuvaki, mother of prince Tivara. Kumaradevi was the Lichchhavi wife of Chandragupta I.

qs.q: Which Ashokan rock edict prohibits animal sacrifice and festive gatherings?
qs.e: Edict I bans animal sacrifice, Edict II provides medical aid, Edict XII preaches tolerance and Edict XIII describes Kalinga.

qs.q: Ashoka sent which two of his children to spread Buddhism in Sri Lanka?
qs.e: His son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra led the mission to Sri Lanka after the Third Buddhist Council.

qs.q: The Mauryan official called the Akaradhyaksha was in charge of:
qs.e: Akara means mine. Navadhyaksha looked after shipping, Samsthadhyaksha markets and Pautavadhyaksha weights.

qs.q: 'Buddhacharita', a Sanskrit life of the Buddha, was written by:
qs.e: Ashvaghosha, who lived at Kanishka's court, wrote the Buddhacharita and was vice-president of the Fourth Buddhist Council.

qs.q: The Tamil epic 'Silappadikaram' was composed by:
qs.e: Ilango Adigal wrote Silappadikaram; Sattanar wrote Manimekalai, the other great Sangam epic.

qs.q: 'Manimekalai', a Sangam-age Buddhist epic, was written by:
