qs.e: Sattanar composed Manimekalai as a sequel to Silappadikaram.

qs.q: The Sangam assemblies of Tamil poets were held under the patronage of which dynasty?
qs.e: The three Sangams were held at Madurai under Pandya patronage, which is why Madurai is the Sangam city.

qs.q: The physician Charaka, author of the Charaka Samhita, was patronised by:
qs.e: Charaka was a court physician of Kanishka, who also patronised Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna.

qs.q: The railings of the Bharhut stupa, carved with Jataka scenes, belong to which period?
qs.e: Bharhut in Madhya Pradesh has Sunga-period railings, just as the Sungas added the railings at Sanchi.

qs.q: Brahmagupta's major work on mathematics and astronomy is:
qs.e: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphuta Siddhanta gave the first clear rules for calculating with zero.

qs.q: 'Panchasiddhantika' and 'Brihat Samhita' were written by:
qs.e: Varahamihira, one of the nine gems, wrote both. Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya.

qs.q: Which Gupta ruler was the first of the line to take the title 'Maharajadhiraja'?
qs.e: Chandragupta I took the grand title and started the Gupta era in 319–20 CE; his predecessors used only 'Maharaja'.

qs.q: The 'nine gems' or navaratnas of the court, said to include Kalidasa, are associated with:
qs.e: Tradition places the navaratnas, Kalidasa and Varahamihira among them, at the court of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya.

qs.q: The iron pillar at Mehrauli in Delhi, famous for resisting rust, is attributed to:
qs.e: Its inscription names a king 'Chandra', generally identified with Chandragupta II, and shows Gupta skill in metallurgy.

qs.q: Pulakeshin II, who defeated Harshavardhana, belonged to which dynasty?
qs.e: Pulakeshin II was a Chalukya of Vatapi (Badami); his victory is recorded in the Aihole inscription of Ravikirti.

qs.q: The capital of the Rashtrakuta dynasty was:
qs.e: Manyakheta (Malkhed) was the Rashtrakuta capital. Vatapi was Chalukyan and Kanchipuram Pallava.

qs.q: The Hoysaleshwara temple at Halebid and the Chennakeshava temple at Belur were built by the:
qs.e: These star-shaped Vesara temples are Hoysala work, now UNESCO World Heritage sites.

qs.q: Which Chola ruler assumed the title 'Gangaikonda Chola' after his northern campaign?
qs.e: Rajendra I reached the Ganga and took the title; he also built a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram.

qs.q: In Chola administration, the largest territorial division was called a:
qs.e: The Chola order ran Mandalam (province), then Valanadu and Nadu, down to the Ur or village.

qs.q: Which is regarded as the oldest university of ancient India?
qs.e: Takshashila is the oldest centre of learning; Nalanda was founded later by Kumaragupta I and Vikramashila by Dharmapala.

qs.q: Sindh was conquered by the Arabs in 712 CE under:
qs.e: Muhammad bin Qasim defeated Raja Dahir in 712 CE; the Chachnama records the conquest.

qs.q: The First Battle of Tarain (1191) was won by:
qs.e: Prithviraj Chauhan won in 1191; Ghori won the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192.

qs.q: The Second Battle of Tarain was fought in:
qs.e: 1192 — Ghori's victory over Prithviraj Chauhan laid the foundation of Turkish rule in India.

qs.q: Al-Beruni, author of Kitab-ul-Hind, came to India with:
qs.e: Al-Beruni accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni and wrote Tahqiq-i-Hind (Kitab-ul-Hind).

qs.q: Mahmud of Ghazni plundered the Somnath temple in:
qs.e: The Somnath raid of 1025 was the most famous of his seventeen invasions.

qs.q: The Battle of Chandawar (1194) was fought between Muhammad Ghori and:
qs.e: Ghori defeated Jaichand of Kannauj at Chandawar two years after Tarain II.

qs.q: 'Prithviraj Raso' was composed by:
qs.e: Chand Bardai, Prithviraj Chauhan's court poet, wrote it in Brajbhasha.

qs.q: The first official history of the Delhi Sultanate, Taj-ul-Maasir, was written by:
qs.e: Hasan Nizami's Taj-ul-Maasir covers the earliest Sultanate years.

qs.q: Firdausi, author of the Shahnama, was a court poet of:
qs.e: Firdausi served at Mahmud of Ghazni's court at Ghazni.

qs.q: Sindh is often called 'the gateway of Islam in India' because:
o: It was the first Indian region to be conquered by the Arabs
It had the first mosque in India
It was Mahmud of Ghazni's first target
qs.e: The Arab conquest of 712 CE made Sindh the first Indian territory under Muslim rule.

qs.q: Muhammad bin Qasim defeated which ruler of Sindh in 712 CE?
qs.e: Raja Dahir of Sindh was defeated and killed at Rawar.

qs.q: How many times did Mahmud of Ghazni invade India?
qs.e: He raided India about seventeen times between 1000 and 1027 CE, mainly for plunder.

qs.q: Which battle in 1192 is regarded as the real foundation of Turkish rule in India?
qs.e: After Tarain II, Ghori's general Qutb-ud-din Aibak established Turkish power in north India.

qs.q: Al-Beruni is sometimes described as the:
qs.e: His Kitab-ul-Hind studied Indian society, science and religion at first hand.

qs.q: Who founded the Delhi Sultanate after the death of Muhammad Ghori in 1206?
qs.e: Aibak, Ghori's slave and general, declared himself independent in 1206.

qs.q: The Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206 by:
qs.e: Aibak, Ghori's slave general, founded the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty in 1206.

qs.q: The construction of the Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak and completed by:
qs.e: Iltutmish completed it; Firoz Shah Tughlaq later repaired it after lightning damage.

qs.q: Who introduced the Iqta system in India?
qs.e: Iltutmish introduced the Iqta — a revenue assignment in place of a cash salary.

qs.q: The silver Tanka and the copper Jital were introduced by:
qs.e: Iltutmish issued the silver tanka and copper jital, giving the Sultanate a standard currency.

qs.q: The only woman ever to sit on the throne of Delhi was:
qs.e: Razia Sultan, daughter of Iltutmish, ruled from 1236 to 1240.

qs.q: Which Sultan took the title 'Zil-i-Ilahi' (Shadow of God)?
qs.e: Balban developed the theory of divine kingship with the titles Zil-i-Ilahi and Niyabat-i-Khudai.

qs.q: The court practices of Sijda and Paibos were introduced by:
qs.e: Sijda was prostration before the Sultan and Paibos the kissing of his feet.

qs.q: Alauddin Khalji's market control was supervised by an officer called the:
qs.e: The Shahna-i-Mandi was the superintendent of markets under the Diwan-i-Riyasat.

qs.q: Who established the first permanent standing army in medieval India?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji raised a permanent standing army paid in cash, with dagh (branding) and huliya (descriptive rolls).

qs.q: Alauddin Khalji raised the land revenue demand to:
qs.e: He fixed it at half the produce and measured land (zabti) to assess it.

qs.q: Malik Kafur was the general who led the southern campaigns of:
qs.e: Malik Kafur carried Khalji arms to Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.

qs.q: Qutb-ud-din Aibak was called 'Lakh Baksh' because he:
qs.e: Lakh Baksh means 'giver of lakhs', a reference to his generosity.

qs.q: The Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer was built by:
qs.e: Aibak built it, along with the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at Delhi.

qs.q: The Turkan-i-Chahalgani, or corps of forty nobles, was created by:
qs.e: Iltutmish created it; Balban later broke its power.

qs.q: Which Sultan assumed the title 'Sikandar-i-Sani' (Second Alexander)?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji took the title, reflecting his ambition of world conquest.

qs.q: Amir Khusrau, called the 'Parrot of India', lived at the court of:
o: Several Sultans from Balban to Muhammad bin Tughlaq
qs.e: He served a succession of Delhi Sultans and was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.

qs.q: Aibak shifted his capital to Lahore; who moved it to Delhi?
qs.e: Iltutmish made Delhi the seat of the Sultanate.

qs.q: Who shifted the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad?
qs.e: Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved it to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, in 1327, and later moved back.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Token currency of brass and copper was introduced by:
qs.e: His token coins of 1329–30 were widely forged and had to be withdrawn.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Diwan-i-Kohi, a department of agriculture, was set up by:
qs.e: It was meant to extend cultivation; Firoz Shah set up the Diwan-i-Khairat and Diwan-i-Bandagan.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Ibn Battuta visited India during the reign of:
qs.e: The Moroccan traveller was made Qazi of Delhi and wrote the Rehla.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Which Sultan was the first to levy jizya on Brahmins?
qs.e: Firoz Shah Tughlaq extended jizya to Brahmins, who had been exempt.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Diwan-i-Khairat, a department of charity, was created by:
qs.e: Firoz Shah also created the Diwan-i-Bandagan for slaves.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Who founded the city of Tughlaqabad?
qs.e: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, the dynasty's founder, built Tughlaqabad.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Timur invaded India in:
qs.e: Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, during the reign of Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Shah Tughlaq.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Sayyid dynasty was founded by:
qs.e: Khizr Khan, Timur's deputy, founded it in 1414 and never took the title Sultan.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The first Afghan dynasty to rule Delhi was the:
qs.e: Bahlol Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451 — the first Afghan dynasty of Delhi.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Who founded the city of Agra in 1504 and made it his capital?
qs.e: Sikandar Lodi founded Agra and introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari for land measurement.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The First Battle of Panipat, in which Ibrahim Lodi was killed, was fought on:
qs.e: Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi on 21 April 1526, ending the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Tarikh-i-Firozshahi was written by:
qs.e: Barani's Tarikh-i-Firozshahi is a major source on Alauddin Khalji and the Tughlaqs.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Sultanate department dealing with royal correspondence was the:
qs.e: Insha = writing. Arz = military, Risalat = religious and foreign affairs, Wizarat = finance.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Which Sultan dug five canals, the largest from the Yamuna to Hisar?
qs.e: Firoz Shah's canals and new towns — Firozabad, Fatehabad, Hisar, Jaunpur — made him the 'builder Sultan'.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The administrative units of the Delhi Sultanate, from largest to smallest, were:
qs.e: Suba–Sarkar–Pargana–Mauza is the Mughal order; the Sultanate used Iqta, Shiq, Pargana and Gram.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 by:
qs.e: The brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya founded it on the Tungabhadra; the capital was Hampi.

qs.q: The Battle of Talikota (1565) was fought between the Deccan sultanates and:
qs.e: Also called Rakshasa-Tangadi, it destroyed Vijayanagara's power under Ramaraya.

qs.q: 'Amuktamalyada', a Telugu work, was composed by:
qs.e: Krishnadeva Raya, the greatest Vijayanagara ruler, wrote it himself.

qs.q: The Ashtadiggajas were eight poets at the court of:
qs.e: They were eight Telugu poets, including Allasani Peddana, at Krishnadeva Raya's court.

qs.q: The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347 by:
qs.e: Hasan Gangu took the title Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah; the capital was Gulbarga, later Bidar.

qs.q: Mahmud Gawan was the famous minister of which kingdom?
qs.e: He built the Madrasa at Bidar; his execution on a false charge hastened the kingdom's break-up.

qs.q: The Charminar at Hyderabad was built in 1591 by:
qs.e: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda built the Charminar.

qs.q: The Gol Gumbaz, famous for its huge dome, is at:
qs.e: Muhammad Adil Shah built it at Bijapur; its dome is among the largest in the world.

qs.q: The Bahmani kingdom broke up into how many successor states?
qs.e: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Berar and Bidar — remember BAGHB.

qs.q: Zain-ul-Abidin, called the 'Akbar of Kashmir', was known for:
o: Abolishing jizya and promoting shawl weaving
qs.e: He was a tolerant ruler who abolished jizya and encouraged crafts such as shawl weaving and papier-mâché.

qs.q: The Vijaya Stambha at Chittor was built by:
qs.e: Rana Kumbha of Mewar raised the Tower of Victory at Chittorgarh.

qs.q: Ahmedabad was founded in 1411 by:
qs.e: Ahmad Shah I of the Gujarat sultanate founded the city and gave it his name.

qs.q: The Russian traveller Athanasius Nikitin visited which kingdom?
qs.e: Nikitin travelled in the Bahmani kingdom in the 15th century.

qs.q: The four dynasties of Vijayanagara, in order, were:
qs.e: Remember SA-SA-TU-AR. Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva line.

qs.q: The gold coin of the Vijayanagara empire was called the:
qs.e: The varaha, called the pagoda by Europeans, was the Vijayanagara gold coin.

qs.q: The Advaita (non-dualist) philosophy was propounded by:
qs.e: Shankara taught Advaita; Ramanuja Vishishtadvaita, Madhva Dvaita and Vallabha Shuddhadvaita.

qs.q: Ramanuja is associated with which school of philosophy?
The Lingayat or Virashaiva movement in Karnataka was led by:
qs.e: Basava led the Lingayats and composed vachanas in Kannada.

qs.q: Which saint is associated with the Nirguna (formless) school of Bhakti?
qs.e: Kabir, Nanak, Ravidas and Dadu are Nirguna; Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira and Chaitanya are Saguna.

qs.q: The Ramcharitmanas was written by:
qs.e: Tulsidas composed the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi during Akbar's reign.

qs.q: Sursagar was composed by:
qs.e: Surdas, the blind poet of Krishna devotion, wrote Sursagar and Sahitya Lahari in Brajbhasha.

qs.q: The Chishti order of Sufism was brought to India by:
qs.e: Moinuddin Chishti settled at Ajmer; the Chishti order became the most popular in India.

qs.q: The Suhrawardi Sufi order in India was founded by:
qs.e: Bahauddin Zakariya established it at Multan; unlike the Chishtis, the Suhrawardis accepted state service.

qs.q: The dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya is at:
qs.e: Nizamuddin Auliya's dargah is in Delhi; Moinuddin Chishti's is at Ajmer.

qs.q: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu popularised which form of worship?
qs.e: Chaitanya spread Krishna devotion in Bengal through collective singing.

qs.q: Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, was born at:
qs.e: He was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.

qs.q: Vaishnavism in Assam was spread by:
qs.e: Shankaradeva also began the Sattriya dance and Borgeet songs.

qs.q: 'Jnaneshwari', a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, was written by:
qs.e: Jnaneshwar's Jnaneshwari is a landmark of Marathi devotional literature.

qs.q: Who was the guru of both Kabir and Ravidas?
qs.e: Ramananda first carried the Bhakti message to north India in the people's language.

qs.q: In Sufi terminology, a 'khanqah' is a:
o: Hospice where a Sufi master lived and taught
qs.e: Khanqah = hospice; Urs = death anniversary; Sama = music and dance; Silsila = order.

qs.q: The Naqshbandi order, which opposed liberal religious policies, is linked with:
qs.e: Ahmad Sirhindi led the orthodox Naqshbandi reaction against Akbar's liberalism.

qs.q: Mirabai's devotional songs were addressed to:
qs.e: Mirabai of Mewar composed padas in Rajasthani and Braj in praise of Krishna.

qs.q: The Battle of Khanwa (1527) was fought between Babur and:
qs.e: Babur's four victories ran Panipat (1526), Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529).

qs.q: Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah Suri at Chausa in:
qs.e: Chausa was in 1539 and Kannauj (Bilgram) in 1540, after which Humayun fled to Persia.

qs.q: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was fought between Hemu and:
qs.e: Bairam Khan, Akbar's regent, defeated Hemu and restored Mughal rule.

qs.q: Sher Shah Suri's original name was:
qs.e: He was named Farid Khan; 'Sher Khan' was a title earned for killing a tiger.

qs.q: The silver Rupiya, ancestor of the modern rupee, was introduced by:
qs.e: Sher Shah issued the silver rupiya of 178 grains and the copper dam.

qs.q: Sher Shah Suri's tomb is at:
qs.e: His octagonal tomb stands in a lake at Sasaram; he died besieging Kalinjar in 1545.

qs.q: The Grand Trunk Road, or Sadak-e-Azam, was rebuilt by:
qs.e: Sher Shah rebuilt it from Sonargaon in Bengal to the Indus, with sarais along the way.

qs.q: Patta and Qabuliyat, documents of land revenue, were introduced by:
qs.e: Patta was the title deed and Qabuliyat the peasant's deed of agreement.

qs.q: Akbar's Dahsala or Zabti revenue system was worked out by:
qs.e: The Dahsala system of 1580 used ten-year averages of yields and prices.

qs.q: Under the Mansabdari system, the rank indicating personal status was:
qs.e: Zat fixed personal rank and pay; Sawar fixed the number of horsemen to be maintained.

qs.q: Akbar abolished jizya in:
qs.e: He abolished jizya in 1564 and the pilgrimage tax in 1563; Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in 1679.

qs.q: The Ibadat Khana, a hall for religious discussion, was built by Akbar at:
qs.e: He built it in 1575 at Fatehpur Sikri and proclaimed Din-i-Ilahi in 1582.

qs.q: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was built to commemorate Akbar's victory over:
qs.e: It was raised in 1573–76 to mark the conquest of Gujarat.

qs.q: The Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari were written by:
qs.e: Abul Fazl, one of Akbar's nine jewels, wrote both.

qs.q: Which two Mughal emperors wrote their own memoirs?
qs.e: Baburnama (in Turki) and Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (in Persian). Akbar was illiterate, so Abul Fazl wrote for him.

qs.q: Humayun-nama was written by:
Humayun's tomb in Delhi was built by:
qs.e: His widow Hamida Banu Begum (Haji Begum) had it built; it is India's first garden tomb.

qs.q: Captain William Hawkins came to the court of:
qs.e: Hawkins arrived in 1608 and Sir Thomas Roe in 1615, both under Jahangir.

qs.q: The 'chain of justice' (zanjir-i-adl) at Agra fort was set up by:
qs.e: Any petitioner could pull the chain to seek the emperor's justice directly.

qs.q: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah at Agra was built by:
qs.e: Nur Jahan built it for her father; it is the first Mughal building fully in marble, with pietra dura work.

qs.q: Mughal painting reached its peak under:
qs.e: Painting peaked under Jahangir (Ustad Mansur, Abul Hasan) while architecture peaked under Shah Jahan.

qs.q: The architect of the Taj Mahal is believed to be:
qs.e: Ustad Ahmad Lahauri is credited as the chief architect; the Taj was built for Mumtaz Mahal.

qs.q: Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in:
qs.e: He reimposed it in 1679, 115 years after Akbar abolished it.

qs.q: Which Mughal emperor was called 'Zinda Pir' (the living saint)?
qs.e: Aurangzeb, who took the title Alamgir, was known for his austere personal life.

qs.q: Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad was built by:
qs.e: Often called the 'mini Taj', it was built for Aurangzeb's wife Dilras Banu Begum.

qs.q: Guru Arjan Dev was executed during the reign of:
qs.e: Guru Arjan Dev was executed by Jahangir in 1606; Guru Tegh Bahadur by Aurangzeb in 1675.

qs.q: Babur was a descendant of Genghis Khan on his:
qs.e: He descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's.

qs.q: The head of the military department in the Mughal administration was the:
qs.e: Mir Bakhshi headed the army and intelligence; the Wazir (Diwan-i-Ala) headed finance.

qs.q: The Mughal officer in charge of the royal household and karkhanas was the:
qs.e: Mir Saman or Khan-i-Saman looked after the imperial household establishments.

qs.q: The Mughal official who acted as censor of public morals was the:
qs.e: The Muhtasib enforced moral regulations; the Qazi-ul-Quzat was the chief judge.

qs.q: The Mughal administrative units, from largest to smallest, were:
Land whose revenue went directly to the imperial treasury was called:
qs.e: Khalisa was crown land; a jagir was assigned to an officer in place of salary.

qs.q: A hereditary homeland jagir held by a Rajput chief was called a:
qs.e: Watan jagirs were not transferable, unlike ordinary jagirs.

qs.q: Akbar's land classification 'Polaj' referred to land that was:
o: Fallow for two to three years
Fallow for five years or more
qs.e: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar and Banjar were the four classes in that order.

qs.q: The revenue method based on sharing the actual crop was called:
qs.e: Ghalla-bakshi was crop sharing; Kankut was an estimate by eye and Nasaq a rough calculation from past figures.

qs.q: Sir Thomas Roe came to Jahangir's court in 1615 as the ambassador of:
qs.e: He secured trading rights for the English at Surat.

qs.q: Francois Bernier, the French traveller, visited India during the reign of:
qs.e: His Travels in the Mogul Empire is a major source on the later Mughal economy.

qs.q: Which French traveller and jeweller described the Peacock Throne?
qs.e: Tavernier, a gem merchant, left a detailed description of the throne.

qs.q: The first Englishman to visit India, during Akbar's reign, was:
qs.e: Ralph Fitch travelled in India in the 1580s under Akbar.

qs.q: The farman of 1717, called the 'Magna Carta of the East India Company', was granted by:
qs.e: Farrukhsiyar's farman gave the Company wide trade concessions in Bengal.

qs.q: Nadir Shah invaded India in 1739 during the reign of:
qs.e: He defeated Muhammad Shah at Karnal and carried away the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor.

qs.q: The Sayyid brothers, who made and unmade emperors, were known as:
qs.e: Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali Khan dominated the court after Bahadur Shah I.

qs.q: The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, was exiled to:
qs.e: He was exiled to Rangoon after 1857 and died there in 1862.

qs.q: The Battle of Buxar (1764) took place during the reign of which Mughal emperor?
qs.e: Shah Alam II himself fought on the losing side and later granted the Diwani of Bengal.

qs.q: Raja Ram Mohan Roy received the title 'Raja' from:
qs.e: Akbar II conferred the title when sending him to England as his envoy.

qs.q: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 at:
qs.e: Raigad was his capital; Pratapgarh is where he killed Afzal Khan in 1659.

qs.q: Shivaji killed Afzal Khan at:
qs.e: The meeting at Pratapgarh in 1659 ended with Afzal Khan's death.

qs.q: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed between Shivaji and:
qs.e: Shivaji surrendered 23 of his 35 forts under the treaty.

qs.q: Shivaji's council of eight ministers was called the:
qs.e: Ashtapradhan included the Peshwa, Amatya, Sachiv, Mantri, Senapati, Sumant, Nyayadhish and Panditrao.

qs.q: In the Maratha system, 'Chauth' was a tax equal to:
qs.e: Chauth was one-fourth; Sardeshmukhi was an additional one-tenth claimed as a hereditary right.

qs.q: The minister in charge of foreign affairs in the Ashtapradhan was the:
qs.e: Sumant or Dabir handled foreign affairs; Panditrao looked after religion and charity.

qs.q: The first Peshwa to make the office hereditary and powerful was:
qs.e: Balaji Vishwanath (1713–20) secured Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights from the Mughals in 1719.

qs.q: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on 14 January 1761 between the Marathas and:
qs.e: The Marathas under Sadashiv Rao Bhau were crushed; Vishwas Rao was killed.

qs.q: The First Anglo-Maratha War ended with the:
qs.e: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) restored the status quo and gave 20 years of peace.

qs.q: The Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed between the English and:
qs.e: It brought Peshwa Baji Rao II under subsidiary alliance and triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

qs.q: Maratha power effectively ended with the:
qs.e: After the third war Lord Hastings abolished the Peshwaship and annexed its territory.

qs.q: The Gurmukhi script was created by:
qs.e: Guru Angad, the second Guru, gave the Sikhs the Gurmukhi script.

qs.q: Amritsar was founded by:
qs.e: Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, founded Amritsar on land granted by Akbar.

qs.q: The Adi Granth was compiled by:
qs.e: Guru Arjan Dev compiled it and built the Harmandir Sahib; he was executed by Jahangir in 1606.

qs.q: The Khalsa was founded in 1699 at Anandpur Sahib by:
qs.e: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa on Baisakhi and prescribed the five Ks.

qs.q: Which Sikh Guru made the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru?
qs.e: Guru Gobind Singh ended the line of living Gurus in 1708.

qs.q: The Maratha house that ruled at Gwalior was the:
Shivaji's son Sambhaji was executed by:
qs.e: Sambhaji was captured and executed in 1689.

qs.q: The 'Chachnama' is the main source for the history of:
qs.e: The Chachnama records Muhammad bin Qasim's conquest of Sindh in 712 CE and the defeat of Raja Dahir.

qs.q: 'Tabaqat-i-Nasiri' was written by:
qs.e: Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote it in Iltutmish's and Balban's time. Hasan Nizami wrote Taj-ul-Maasir.

qs.q: Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered which two regions for the Turks?
qs.e: He overran Bihar and Bengal and destroyed Nalanda in 1193.

qs.q: Muhammad Ghori died, leaving the way open for Turkish rule in India, in:
qs.e: Ghori died in 1206, and his slave general Qutb-ud-din Aibak then founded the Delhi Sultanate.

qs.q: Mahmud of Ghazni belonged to which dynasty?
qs.e: Mahmud was a Ghaznavid. Muhammad Ghori belonged to the rival Ghurid house that displaced the Ghaznavids.

qs.q: Qutb-ud-din Aibak died in 1210 at Lahore while playing:
qs.e: He fell from his horse during a game of chaugan, the medieval form of polo.

qs.q: The Qutub Minar was raised in honour of which Sufi saint?
qs.e: Aibak dedicated it to Bakhtiyar Kaki of Delhi, the successor of Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer.

qs.q: Iltutmish obtained a khilat, a letter of recognition as Sultan, in 1229 from the:
qs.e: The Caliph's recognition made Iltutmish the legal sovereign of Delhi and gave the Sultanate standing.

qs.q: Who founded the Khalji dynasty in 1290?
qs.e: Jalal-ud-din Khalji founded it with a mild policy; his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin murdered him in 1296.

qs.q: The Diwan-i-Riyasat, the department supervising commerce and market control, was created by:
qs.e: It worked under Alauddin Khalji's market-control scheme, with the Shahna-i-Mandi as market superintendent.

qs.q: Which Sultan built the Siri fort at Delhi?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji built Siri and the Alai Darwaza as part of his defences against the Mongols.

qs.q: Who described Muhammad bin Tughlaq as 'a mixture of opposites'?
qs.e: Barani, the historian of the Tughlaq court, used the phrase for the learned but unlucky Sultan.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq died in 1325 when:
o: A pavilion collapsed on him at Afghanpur
He was killed fighting the Mongols
qs.e: The wooden pavilion built to welcome him at Afghanpur fell on him; Aibak, by contrast, died playing chaugan.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: 'Futuhat-i-Firozshahi' was written by:
qs.e: The Sultan wrote this account of his own achievements; Afif wrote a separate Tarikh-i-Firozshahi.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Which Sultan had two Ashokan pillars shifted to Delhi?
qs.e: Firoz Shah moved pillars from Topra and Meerut to Delhi and also repaired the Qutub Minar.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Sikandar Lodi wrote Persian verse under which pen name?
qs.e: Sikandar Lodi used the pen name Gulrukhi. Bahadur Shah II wrote as 'Zafar'.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: The Diwan-i-Mustakharaj, a department for arrears of revenue, was set up by:
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji created it to recover revenue arrears; the Diwan-i-Kohi for agriculture was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's.
qs.tag: Delhi Sultanate II — Tughlaq to Lodi

qs.q: Hampi, the capital of Vijayanagara, stood on the banks of which river?
qs.e: Harihara I and Bukka Raya founded the city on the Tungabhadra; its ruins at Hampi are a UNESCO site.

qs.q: The Vittalaswamy and Hazara Rama temples at Hampi were built by:
qs.e: Krishnadeva Raya, the greatest Vijayanagara ruler, built both.

qs.q: Vijayanagara was led at the Battle of Talikota by:
qs.e: Ramaraya of the Aravidu line commanded the Vijayanagara army in 1565 and was killed; Krishnadeva Raya had died in 1529.

qs.q: The Italian traveller Nicolo Conti visited the court of:
qs.e: Nicolo Conti came under Devaraya I, while the Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq came under Devaraya II.

qs.q: Jaunpur, a great centre of learning under the Sharqi rulers, was known as:
qs.e: Jaunpur was called the Shiraz of India for its scholarship; its Atala Masjid is the best-known Sharqi building.

qs.q: The Vijayanagara practice of granting territory to military commanders in return for troops was called the:
qs.e: Under the amara-nayaka system a nayaka held land and maintained soldiers for the king, somewhat like the earlier iqta.

qs.q: The four mathas at Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Badrinath were established by:
qs.e: Shankaracharya, born at Kaladi in Kerala, set up the four mathas and taught Advaita.

qs.q: Who was the only woman among the twelve Alvar saints?
qs.e: Andal of Tamil Nadu was the one woman Alvar. Akka Mahadevi was a woman Lingayat saint of Karnataka.

qs.q: The Pushtimarg sect of Krishna devotion was founded by:
qs.e: Vallabhacharya, who taught Shuddhadvaita, founded the Pushtimarg.

qs.q: The 'Bijak', a collection of verses, is associated with:
qs.e: The Bijak gathers Kabir's dohas and sakhis; some of his verses are also in the Guru Granth Sahib.

qs.q: The dargah of Baba Farid, the Chishti saint, is at:
qs.e: Baba Farid's dargah is at Pakpattan. Ajmer has Moinuddin Chishti's and Delhi Nizamuddin Auliya's.

qs.q: At the Battle of Haldighati in 1576, Akbar's army was led against Maharana Pratap by:
qs.e: Man Singh of Amber commanded the Mughal force; Pratap withdrew but never submitted.

qs.q: The Battle of Samugarh in 1659 was fought between Aurangzeb and:
qs.e: Aurangzeb defeated his eldest brother Dara Shikoh at Samugarh in the war of succession.

qs.q: Babur wrote his memoir, the Baburnama, in which language?
qs.e: Babur wrote in Turki; Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan later translated it into Persian. Jahangir's memoir was in Persian.

qs.q: The only notable follower of Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi was:
qs.e: Din-i-Ilahi, proclaimed in 1582, won almost no converts; Birbal is the one courtier named as joining it.

qs.q: Babur was invited to invade India against Ibrahim Lodi by:
qs.e: Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab, and Alam Khan invited Babur, who then won the First Battle of Panipat.

qs.q: 'Padmavat' was composed during the reign of Sher Shah Suri by:
qs.e: Jayasi wrote the Awadhi poem Padmavat at Sher Shah's time; Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas under Akbar.

qs.q: The Mughal official who kept land records at the village level was the:
qs.e: The Patwari kept village records and the Qanungo those of the pargana; the Amil collected revenue.

qs.q: The head of the city police in Mughal administration was the:
qs.e: The Kotwal policed the city, while the Faujdar had charge of a sarkar or district.

qs.q: Which later Mughal emperor was nicknamed 'Shah-i-Bekhabar'?
qs.e: Bahadur Shah I was called the heedless king. Muhammad Shah was nicknamed 'Rangila'.

qs.q: Niccolao Manucci, who wrote 'Storia do Mogor', came from:
qs.e: Manucci was Italian. Bernier and Tavernier were French, and Hawkins and Roe English.

qs.q: A revenue-free grant made to scholars and religious men was called:
qs.e: Inam was revenue-free. A jagir carried a revenue assignment for service, and khalisa land paid into the treasury.

qs.q: Shivaji's mother and his spiritual guru were:
qs.e: His mother was Jijabai and his guru Samarth Ramdas, author of Dasbodh; Dadaji Kondadev was his teacher.

qs.q: Shivaji plundered the rich Mughal port of Surat in:
qs.e: He raided Surat in 1664, a year after attacking Shaista Khan at Pune.

qs.q: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, the minister in charge of justice was the:
qs.e: Nyayadhish handled justice and Panditrao religion and charity; the Sachiv looked after correspondence.

qs.q: Who led the Sikhs against the Mughals after the death of Guru Gobind Singh in 1708?
qs.e: Banda Bahadur fought the Mughals from 1708 to 1716; Ranjit Singh built the Sikh kingdom much later.

qs.q: The Akal Takht at Amritsar was established by:
qs.e: The sixth Guru, Hargobind, built the Akal Takht and adopted the two swords of miri and piri.

qs.q: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in:
qs.e: He landed at Calicut in May 1498 and was received by the Zamorin.

qs.q: The first Portuguese Viceroy in India was:
qs.e: Almeida was the first Viceroy; Albuquerque, who took Goa in 1510, is called the real founder of Portuguese power.

qs.q: The English East India Company received its charter in 1600 from:
qs.e: Elizabeth I granted the charter on 31 December 1600.

qs.q: Fort St George was built by the English at:
qs.e: Fort St George–Madras (1639), Fort William–Calcutta (1690), Fort St David–Cuddalore.

qs.q: Calcutta was founded in 1690 by:
qs.e: Job Charnock established the English settlement that became Calcutta.

qs.q: Bombay was transferred to the English East India Company in 1668 by:
qs.e: Charles II received it as dowry from Portugal and leased it to the Company for £10 a year.

qs.q: The Dutch were defeated by the English at the Battle of Bedara in:
qs.e: Bedara ended Dutch ambitions in India; Wandiwash (1760) ended French ones.

qs.q: The French East India Company was founded in 1664 under:
qs.e: Colbert founded it during the reign of Louis XIV; Pondicherry became its headquarters in 1674.

qs.q: The Third Carnatic War was decided by the Battle of:
qs.e: Eyre Coote defeated Count de Lally at Wandiwash in 1760; the Treaty of Paris followed in 1763.

qs.q: The Battle of Plassey was fought on:
qs.e: Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, who had been betrayed by Mir Jafar.

qs.q: Who betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah at the Battle of Plassey?
qs.e: Mir Jafar, the commander, defected and was made Nawab after the battle.

qs.q: The Battle of Buxar (1764) was won for the English by:
qs.e: Munro defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II.

qs.q: The Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha were granted to the Company in 1765 by:
qs.e: Shah Alam II granted the right to collect revenue after the Treaty of Allahabad.

qs.q: The dual government in Bengal was introduced by:
qs.e: Clive set it up in 1765; Warren Hastings ended it in 1772.

qs.q: Which European power was the first to arrive in India and the last to leave?
qs.e: They came in 1498; Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated only in 1961.

qs.q: The Danish established their first factory in India at:
qs.e: The Danes settled at Tranquebar (1620) and Serampore, and sold their holdings to the English in 1845.

qs.q: Mir Qasim came into conflict with the Company chiefly over:
o: Misuse of the dastak (free trade pass)
qs.e: He abolished all inland duties so that Indian traders were not disadvantaged, which angered the Company.

qs.q: Tipu Sultan died fighting the British in:
qs.e: He died defending Seringapatam on 4 May 1799 in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

qs.q: The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) was signed after the:
qs.e: Cornwallis forced Tipu to give up half his territory.

qs.q: The Subsidiary Alliance system was introduced by:
qs.e: Wellesley introduced it in 1798; Hyderabad was the first state to sign.

qs.q: Which state was the first to accept the Subsidiary Alliance?
qs.e: Hyderabad signed in 1798, followed by Mysore (1799) and Awadh (1801).

qs.q: The Doctrine of Lapse was applied by:
qs.e: Dalhousie annexed states whose rulers died without a natural heir.

qs.q: The first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse was:
qs.e: Satara fell in 1848, then Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat, Udaipur, Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).

qs.q: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of:
qs.e: Awadh was taken on the charge of misgovernment, not under the Doctrine of Lapse — a standard trap.

qs.q: Punjab was annexed by the British after the:
qs.e: Punjab was annexed in 1849 after the second war; the Koh-i-Noor was taken to England.

qs.q: By the Treaty of Amritsar (1846), Kashmir was sold to:
qs.e: Gulab Singh of Jammu bought Kashmir for 75 lakh rupees, founding the Dogra dynasty.

qs.q: The Treaty of Sugauli (1816) was signed with:
qs.e: It ended the Anglo-Nepal War and gave the British Shimla, Kumaon and Garhwal, plus Gurkha recruitment.

qs.q: The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the war with:
qs.e: It concluded the First Anglo-Burmese War.

qs.q: Sindh was annexed in 1843 by:
qs.e: Charles Napier led the conquest under Governor-General Ellenborough.

qs.q: India's first railway ran in 1853 between:
qs.e: The 34-km Bombay–Thane line opened on 16 April 1853 under Dalhousie.

qs.q: Wood's Despatch (1854) is called the:
o: Magna Carta of English education in India
qs.e: Sir Charles Wood's Despatch laid out a complete plan for education in India.

qs.q: Haidar Ali died during the:
qs.e: He died in 1782, and Tipu Sultan carried on the second war, ending it with the Treaty of Mangalore.

qs.q: The first Governor-General of Bengal was:
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 created the office, and Warren Hastings was the first holder.

qs.q: The first Governor-General of India was:
qs.e: The Charter Act of 1833 created the post, and Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India.

qs.q: Who was both the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1858 changed his title during his term.

qs.q: Sati was abolished in 1829 by:
qs.e: Bentinck passed Regulation XVII of 1829, backed by Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign.

qs.q: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal was introduced in 1793 by:
qs.e: Cornwallis fixed the zamindars as proprietors with a revenue demand fixed for ever.

qs.q: Lord Cornwallis is known as the:
o: Father of the Indian civil services
qs.e: He reorganised the services and separated revenue from justice.

qs.q: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 during the governor-generalship of:
qs.e: Sir William Jones founded it with Warren Hastings' support.

qs.q: The first census of India was conducted in 1872 under:
qs.e: The 1872 census was non-synchronous; the first synchronous census was in 1881 under Ripon.

qs.q: Which Viceroy was assassinated in office?
qs.e: Lord Mayo was killed in the Andamans in 1872 — the only Viceroy murdered in office.

qs.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was passed by:
qs.e: Lytton passed it and Ripon repealed it in 1882.

qs.q: Lord Ripon is remembered as the Father of:
qs.e: His resolution of 1882 gave India elected local bodies.

qs.q: The Indian National Congress was founded during the viceroyalty of:
qs.e: The Congress was founded in December 1885 when Dufferin was Viceroy.

qs.q: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 was carried out by:
qs.e: Curzon ordered it; Hardinge II annulled it in 1911.

qs.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced by the:
qs.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1909, under Minto II, introduced separate electorates.

qs.q: The capital of British India was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in:
qs.e: It was announced at the Delhi Durbar of 1911 under Lord Hardinge II; New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931.

qs.q: The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, which reorganised the ASI, was passed in 1904 by:
qs.e: Curzon's Act of 1904 gave the Archaeological Survey its modern footing.

qs.q: The Quit India Movement took place during the viceroyalty of:
qs.e: Linlithgow was Viceroy in 1942; Wavell followed in 1943.

qs.q: The Cabinet Mission came to India during the viceroyalty of:
qs.e: The Cabinet Mission arrived in March 1946 under Wavell.

qs.q: The first and only Indian Governor-General of India was:
qs.e: Rajagopalachari held the office from 1948 to 1950, when India became a republic.

qs.q: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on:
qs.e: Signed by Gandhi and Viceroy Irwin, it suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement.

qs.q: The immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857 was:
o: The greased cartridges of the Enfield P-53 rifle
qs.e: The cartridges were said to be greased with cow and pig fat, offending both Hindu and Muslim sepoys.

qs.q: Mangal Pandey's revolt took place at:
qs.e: He fired on his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was hanged on 8 April.

qs.q: The Revolt of 1857 broke out in full at Meerut on:
qs.e: The Meerut sepoys rose on 10 May and reached Delhi on 11 May.

qs.q: The leader of the revolt at Lucknow was:
qs.e: Begum Hazrat Mahal led Lucknow on behalf of her son Birjis Qadr.

qs.q: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi was finally defeated by:
qs.e: Hugh Rose pursued her; she died fighting near Gwalior in June 1858.

qs.q: The real name of Tantia Tope was:
qs.e: Tantia Tope was Nana Saheb's general; Nana Saheb's own name was Dhondu Pant.

qs.q: The revolt at Arrah in Bihar was led by:
qs.e: The octogenarian zamindar Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur led it with his brother Amar Singh.

qs.q: Who led the sepoys at Delhi during the revolt?
qs.e: Bakht Khan commanded the sepoys at Delhi, with Bahadur Shah II as figurehead.

qs.q: Who described the Revolt of 1857 as the 'First War of Indian Independence'?
qs.e: Savarkar's book of that title gave the phrase currency; John Lawrence called it a mere sepoy mutiny.

qs.q: The Government of India Act 1858 created the office of:
o: Viceroy's Executive Council member for law
qs.e: It transferred power to the Crown, created the Secretary of State with a 15-member Council, and made the Governor-General Viceroy.

qs.q: The Queen's Proclamation of 1 November 1858 was read out at:
qs.e: Lord Canning read it at Allahabad, promising no further annexations and respect for Indian religions.

qs.q: The leader of the revolt at Bareilly was:
qs.e: Khan Bahadur Khan led Bareilly; Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah led Faizabad.

qs.q: Which of these regions remained largely unaffected by the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: Punjab, Sindh, Rajputana, Kashmir, Bengal and most of the south stayed quiet.

qs.q: The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856, a military cause of the revolt, required sepoys to:
qs.e: Many sepoys regarded crossing the sea as loss of caste.

qs.q: The Revolt of 1857 was officially declared over on:
qs.e: Lord Canning declared peace on 8 July 1858.

qs.q: Which commission reorganised the Indian army after 1857?
qs.e: The Peel Commission (1859) raised the ratio of European to Indian troops and kept artillery with Europeans.

qs.q: The Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1828 by:
qs.e: Ram Mohan Roy founded it at Calcutta; Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen led it later.

qs.q: The Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 by:
qs.e: Its slogan was 'Back to the Vedas' and its main text Satyarth Prakash.

qs.q: 'Satyarth Prakash' was written by:
qs.e: It sets out the Arya Samaj's teaching against idol worship and caste.

qs.q: The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897 by:
qs.e: Vivekananda founded it at Belur in memory of his guru Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.

qs.q: Swami Vivekananda addressed the Parliament of Religions at Chicago in:
qs.e: His speech of 1893 made him famous; his birthday, 12 January, is National Youth Day.

qs.q: The Theosophical Society was founded in 1875 in:
qs.e: Blavatsky and Olcott founded it in New York; the Indian headquarters moved to Adyar, Madras, in 1882.

qs.q: The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by:
qs.e: Phule founded it at Pune in 1873 and wrote Gulamgiri.

qs.q: Raja Ram Mohan Roy's Bengali journal was:
qs.e: He also published Mirat-ul-Akhbar in Persian.

qs.q: The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 was the result of the efforts of:
qs.e: Vidyasagar campaigned for it; Malabari secured the Age of Consent Act of 1891.

qs.q: The Age of Consent Act of 1891 was passed through the efforts of:
qs.e: It raised the age of consent for girls to twelve.

qs.q: The Aligarh Movement was led by:
qs.e: He founded the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College in 1875, which became AMU in 1920.

qs.q: The Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu was started by:
qs.e: Periyar launched it in 1925 against caste and Brahmin dominance.

qs.q: The Servants of India Society was founded in 1905 by:
qs.e: Gokhale founded it at Bombay to train national workers.

qs.q: The slogan 'One caste, one religion, one God for mankind' was given by:
qs.e: Sree Narayana Guru founded the SNDP Yogam in Kerala in 1903.

qs.q: The Young Bengal Movement was led by:
qs.e: Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College, inspired a group of radical young thinkers.

qs.q: The Prarthana Samaj was founded at Bombay in 1867 by:
qs.e: Atmaram Pandurang founded it; Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar made it influential.

qs.q: Raja Ram Mohan Roy is called the:
qs.e: Tilak was called the Father of Indian unrest and Naoroji the Grand Old Man of India.

qs.q: The Bahishkrit Hitkarini Sabha was founded in 1924 by:
qs.e: Ambedkar founded it at Bombay; his papers included Mooknayak and Bahishkrit Bharat.

qs.q: Sharda Sadan, a home for widows, was founded by:
qs.e: Pandita Ramabai founded it in 1889 and also started the Arya Mahila Samaj.

qs.q: The Sarda Act of 1929 dealt with:
qs.e: The Child Marriage Restraint Act set the marriage age at 14 for girls and 18 for boys.

qs.q: The Indian National Congress was founded on:
qs.e: It met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, with 72 delegates.

qs.q: The founder of the Indian National Congress was:
qs.e: A. O. Hume, a retired civil servant, founded it; W. C. Bonnerjee was the first President.

qs.q: The first President of the Indian National Congress was:
qs.e: Womesh Chandra Banerjee presided over the Bombay session of 1885.

qs.q: The Indian Association was founded in 1876 by:
o: Surendranath Banerjee and Anand Mohan Bose
qs.e: It was the most important pre-Congress political body in Bengal.

qs.q: The East India Association was founded in London in 1866 by:
qs.e: Naoroji founded it to put the Indian case before the British public.

qs.q: The 'Drain Theory' was put forward by:
qs.e: He set it out in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901).

qs.q: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' was the declaration of:
qs.e: Tilak was the first to demand swaraj outright.

qs.q: Tilak's two newspapers were:
qs.e: Kesari was in Marathi and Maratha in English.

qs.q: The Partition of Bengal took effect on:
qs.e: The day was observed across Bengal as a day of mourning, and the Swadeshi movement began.

qs.q: The Muslim League was founded in 1906 at:
qs.e: Nawab Salimullah of Dhaka and the Aga Khan founded it.

qs.q: The Congress split into Moderates and Extremists at the session of:
qs.e: The Surat Split of 1907 divided the Congress for nine years.

qs.q: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was significant because it:
o: Brought the Congress and the Muslim League together and reunited the Congress
qs.e: It achieved both Hindu-Muslim cooperation and the reunion of Moderates and Extremists.

qs.q: Who was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: Annie Besant presided at Calcutta in 1917; Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman President, in 1925.

qs.q: The first Indian woman to preside over a Congress session was:
qs.e: Sarojini Naidu presided at Kanpur in 1925.

qs.q: Who was the only person to be Congress President three times in the early period?
The first Muslim President of the Congress was:
qs.e: Badruddin Tyabji presided over the Madras session of 1887.

qs.q: The Home Rule League was started in Madras in September 1916 by:
qs.e: Tilak's League was started at Pune in April 1916 and Besant's at Madras in September.

qs.q: The Congress session that adopted Purna Swaraj as its goal was held at:
qs.e: Nehru presided; the tricolour was hoisted on the Ravi on 31 December 1929.

qs.q: The resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme was passed at the Congress session of:
qs.e: Sardar Patel presided over the Karachi session of 1931.

qs.q: Subhas Chandra Bose resigned as Congress President in 1939 and founded the:
qs.e: He resigned after winning at Tripuri against Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya.

qs.q: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India was at:
qs.e: The Champaran satyagraha of 1917 was against the tinkathia indigo system in Bihar.

qs.q: Gandhi was invited to Champaran by:
qs.e: The local cultivator Rajkumar Shukla persuaded him to come.

qs.q: Gandhi's first hunger strike in India was during the:
qs.e: He fasted in support of the Ahmedabad mill workers in 1918.

qs.q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on:
qs.e: General Dyer ordered the firing at Amritsar on Baisakhi day.

qs.q: Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest against:
qs.e: He returned the knighthood in 1919 after the Amritsar massacre.

qs.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after the incident at:
qs.e: Twenty-two policemen were killed at Chauri Chaura on 5 February 1922.

qs.q: The Swaraj Party was founded in 1923 by:
o: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru
qs.e: They wanted to enter the legislative councils and obstruct from within.

qs.q: The Simon Commission was boycotted because:
qs.e: All seven members were British, which led to the cry 'Go back Simon'.

qs.q: Lala Lajpat Rai was fatally injured during a lathi charge while protesting against:
qs.e: He was beaten at Lahore in October 1928 and died soon after.

qs.q: Vallabhbhai Patel earned the title 'Sardar' after leading the:
qs.e: The women of Bardoli gave him the title in 1928.

qs.q: The Dandi March began on:
qs.e: Gandhi set out on 12 March 1930 and broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April.

qs.q: How many followers accompanied Gandhi at the start of the Dandi March?
qs.e: He walked about 385 km from Sabarmati to Dandi with 78 chosen followers.

qs.q: Gandhi attended which Round Table Conference?
qs.e: He attended only the Second Round Table Conference (1931) as the sole Congress representative.

qs.q: The Poona Pact of 1932 was signed between Gandhi and:
qs.e: It replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats.

qs.q: The Communal Award of 1932 was announced by:
qs.e: The British Prime Minister's award gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes.

qs.q: Gandhi presided over only one Congress session, held at:
qs.e: He presided at Belgaum in 1924 — the only time.

qs.q: Gandhi's autobiography is titled:
qs.e: Hind Swaraj (1909) is a separate work; India Wins Freedom is Maulana Azad's.

qs.q: The title 'Mahatma' was given to Gandhi by:
qs.e: Tagore called him Mahatma; Bose called him Father of the Nation.

qs.q: Gandhi's political guru was:
qs.e: Gandhi himself described Gokhale as his political guru.

qs.q: The first Independence Day was observed on:
qs.e: After the Lahore resolution, 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day — which is why 26 January was chosen in 1950.

qs.q: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on:
qs.e: They were executed at Lahore; 23 March is observed as Shaheed Diwas.

qs.q: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly on:
qs.e: They wanted 'to make the deaf hear' and deliberately allowed themselves to be arrested.

qs.q: Chandra Shekhar Azad died fighting the police at:
qs.e: He was killed on 27 February 1931 at Alfred Park (now Chandrashekhar Azad Park).

qs.q: The Kakori Conspiracy case of 1925 involved:
qs.e: Ramprasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged for it.

qs.q: Who among these was hanged in the Kakori case?
qs.e: Remember BARR: Bismil, Ashfaqullah, Roshan Singh, Rajendra Lahiri.

qs.q: The Chittagong Armoury Raid of 1930 was led by:
qs.e: Surya Sen 'Masterda' led it, helped by Kalpana Dutta and Pritilata Waddedar.

qs.q: The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 at:
qs.e: Lala Hardayal and Sohan Singh Bhakna founded it; its paper was called Ghadar.

qs.q: Abhinav Bharat was founded by:
qs.e: Savarkar founded it at Nasik in 1904.

qs.q: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb in 1908 at:
qs.e: They were aiming at the magistrate Kingsford but killed the Kennedys instead.

qs.q: The Indian National Army was first raised in 1942 by:
qs.e: Mohan Singh raised it with Rash Behari Bose's Indian Independence League; Bose took command in 1943.

qs.q: Subhas Chandra Bose took command of the INA at Singapore on:
qs.e: He proclaimed the Azad Hind Government at Singapore on 21 October 1943.

qs.q: The women's regiment of the INA was named after:
qs.e: The Rani Jhansi Regiment was commanded by Captain Lakshmi Sahgal.

qs.q: 'Give me blood and I will give you freedom' was the call of:
qs.e: Bose gave the call to the INA; he also gave the slogans 'Jai Hind' and 'Chalo Delhi'.

qs.q: The Royal Indian Navy mutiny broke out on:
qs.e: The RIN ratings at Bombay mutinied in February 1946.

qs.q: The Quit India Resolution was passed on 8 August 1942 at:
qs.e: Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die'; the leaders were arrested on 9 August.

qs.q: A parallel government during the Quit India Movement was set up at Satara by:
o: Nana Patil and Y. B. Chavan
qs.e: Satara's 'Prati Sarkar' was the longest lasting; Ballia's was led by Chittu Pandey.

qs.q: The Cripps Mission came to India in:
qs.e: Gandhi called its offer of post-war dominion status 'a post-dated cheque'.

qs.q: The three members of the Cabinet Mission were:
o: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander
qs.e: Remember PCA. The Mission arrived in March 1946 and rejected Pakistan.

qs.q: Direct Action Day was observed by the Muslim League on:
qs.e: It led to large-scale killings in Calcutta.

qs.q: The Constituent Assembly of India first met on:
qs.e: Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman; Rajendra Prasad was elected President on 11 December.

qs.q: The Mountbatten Plan for partition was announced on:
qs.e: The Indian Independence Act followed on 18 July 1947.

qs.q: The boundary between India and Pakistan was drawn by:
qs.e: The Radcliffe Commission drew the line in Punjab and Bengal.

qs.q: The first satyagrahi of the Individual Satyagraha of 1940 was:
qs.e: Vinoba Bhave was the first and Nehru the second.

qs.q: Subhas Chandra Bose is said to have died in an air crash at:
The Regulating Act of 1773 created the post of:
qs.e: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal under it.

qs.q: The Board of Control was created by:
qs.e: Pitt's India Act set up the dual government of the Company and the Crown.

qs.q: Which Act first provided a grant for education in India?
qs.e: It set aside one lakh rupees a year for education and allowed missionaries into India.

qs.q: Open competition for the civil services was introduced by the:
qs.e: The 1853 Act also first separated legislative and executive functions.

qs.q: The portfolio system was introduced by the:
qs.e: The 1861 Act also brought Indians into the legislative council by nomination for the first time.

qs.q: Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the:
qs.e: The 1919 Act split provincial subjects into transferred and reserved; the 1935 Act ended provincial dyarchy.

qs.q: Provincial autonomy was introduced by the:
qs.e: The 1935 Act is the main source of the Indian Constitution.

qs.q: The Reserve Bank of India was set up under the:
qs.e: The 1935 Act also provided for a Federal Court, established in 1937.

qs.q: The Permanent Settlement covered roughly what share of British India?
qs.e: Zamindari about 19%, Mahalwari about 30% and Ryotwari about 51% — the largest.

qs.q: The Ryotwari system was introduced by:
qs.e: Munro and Captain Read introduced it in Madras; the settlement was made directly with the cultivator.

qs.q: The Mahalwari system was devised by:
qs.e: Mackenzie introduced it in 1822; Bentinck revised it in 1833. The village or mahal was the unit.

qs.q: 'Nil Darpan', a play exposing the oppression of indigo planters, was written by:
qs.e: It was written in 1860 during the Indigo revolt in Bengal.

qs.q: The Santhal rebellion of 1855–56 was led by:
qs.e: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the Santhal hool in present-day Jharkhand.

qs.q: The Munda rebellion, known as Ulgulan, was led by:
qs.e: Birsa Munda led it in 1899–1900; his birthday, 15 November, is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

qs.q: The All India Kisan Sabha was founded in 1936 by:
qs.e: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was its first president; the Awadh Kisan Sabha of 1918 came earlier.

qs.q: The Moplah revolt of 1921 took place in:
qs.e: The Moplah peasants of Malabar rose against landlords during the Khilafat agitation.

qs.q: The Deccan riots of 1875 were directed mainly against:
qs.e: They led to the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act of 1879.

qs.q: The office of Secretary of State for India was abolished by the:
qs.e: The 1858 Act created it and the 1947 Act abolished it.

qs.q: The Dutch set up their first factory in India at:
qs.e: The Dutch began at Masulipatnam in 1605. Tranquebar was Danish and Pondicherry French.

qs.q: The First Carnatic War ended with the:
qs.e: Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) closed the inconclusive first war; the Treaty of Paris (1763) ended the third.

qs.q: The English East India Company's first factory in India was established in 1613 at:
qs.e: The Surat factory was set up in 1613 under Jahangir, after Hawkins' and Roe's missions.

qs.q: Which French Governor of Pondicherry was recalled after the Second Carnatic War?
qs.e: Dupleix was recalled in 1754. Lally lost at Wandiwash in 1760 and Colbert had founded the French company in 1664.

qs.q: The great Bengal famine in which about a third of the population is said to have died occurred in:
qs.e: The famine of 1770 followed the Company's revenue exactions under the dual government.

qs.q: The First Anglo-Mysore War ended with the:
qs.e: The Treaty of Madras (1769) closed the first war with Haidar Ali; Mangalore ended the second in 1784.

qs.q: The Second Anglo-Mysore War was ended by the Treaty of:
qs.e: Tipu Sultan signed the Treaty of Mangalore in 1784 after Haidar Ali's death in 1782.

qs.q: Tipu Sultan was popularly known as:
qs.e: Tipu was the Tiger of Mysore; Ranjit Singh was the Lion of Punjab and Samudragupta the Indian Napoleon.

qs.q: Which ruling family was restored in Mysore after Tipu Sultan's death in 1799?
qs.e: The Wodeyars were put back on the throne under a subsidiary alliance with Wellesley.

qs.q: Jhansi was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in:
qs.e: Satara went first in 1848, Jhansi in 1853 and Nagpur in 1854; Awadh in 1856 was taken for misgovernment.

qs.q: The Koh-i-Noor diamond was taken to England after the British annexation of:
qs.e: Punjab was annexed in 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War, and the diamond passed from Dalip Singh to the Crown.

qs.q: India's first telegraph line was laid between:
qs.e: Both the first telegraph line (Calcutta-Agra) and the first railway (Bombay-Thane) date from 1853, under Dalhousie.

qs.q: The Supreme Court at Calcutta was set up in 1774 during the time of:
qs.e: It followed the Regulating Act of 1773, under the first Governor-General of Bengal, Warren Hastings.

qs.q: Fort William College at Calcutta was founded in 1800 by:
qs.e: Wellesley founded it to train Company servants in Indian languages.

qs.q: Slavery was abolished in India in 1843 under which Governor-General?
qs.e: Ellenborough, who also annexed Sindh in 1843, abolished slavery. Hardinge I banned human sacrifice.

qs.q: The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in 1857 during the term of:
qs.e: They were set up under Canning, following Wood's Despatch of 1854.

qs.q: The Ilbert Bill controversy arose during the viceroyalty of:
qs.e: Ripon's Ilbert Bill of 1883 sought to let Indian judges try Europeans, and European opposition forced its dilution.

qs.q: The Durand Line between British India and Afghanistan was drawn in 1893 under:
qs.e: Lansdowne's term saw the Durand Line and the Indian Councils Act of 1892.

qs.q: Queen Victoria was proclaimed 'Kaiser-i-Hind' at the Delhi Durbar of 1877 held by:
qs.e: Lytton held the durbar in the middle of a severe famine, and also passed the Vernacular Press and Arms Acts of 1878.

qs.q: Mangal Pandey belonged to which regiment?
qs.e: He served in the 34th Native Infantry at Barrackpore and was hanged on 8 April 1857.

qs.q: Who led the revolt of 1857 at Kanpur?
qs.e: Nana Saheb led Kanpur with his general Tantia Tope; Bakht Khan commanded at Delhi.

qs.q: Which British commander died while defending Lucknow in 1857?
qs.e: Henry Lawrence died in the Lucknow residency; Colin Campbell later relieved the city.

qs.q: Rani Lakshmibai died fighting in June 1858 near:
qs.e: She left Jhansi, joined Tantia Tope and died in action near Gwalior — a point SSC often tests.

qs.q: Who held that the Revolt of 1857 was 'neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence'?
qs.e: R. C. Majumdar rejected all three claims, while Savarkar called it the First War of Indian Independence.

qs.q: The revolt of 1857 at Allahabad was led by:
qs.e: Maulvi Liaquat Ali led Allahabad and was put down by Colonel Neill; Kandarpeshwar Singh led in Assam.

qs.q: The Atmiya Sabha was founded in 1815 by:
qs.e: Ram Mohan Roy founded the Atmiya Sabha first and then the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.

qs.q: The Tattvabodhini Sabha was founded in 1839 by:
qs.e: Debendranath Tagore founded it and later led the Brahmo Samaj; Keshab Chandra Sen formed the Brahmo Samaj of India in 1866.

qs.q: The Deoband movement was started in 1866 by:
o: Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi
qs.e: Deoband was an orthodox movement of religious education, unlike Sir Syed's Aligarh movement of English education.

qs.q: The journal 'Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq' was published by:
qs.e: Sir Syed used it to spread his ideas of social reform and modern education among Muslims.

qs.q: The Central Hindu College at Banaras, which later became the nucleus of Banaras Hindu University, was founded by:
qs.e: Annie Besant founded the college in 1898; Malaviya built BHU on its base in 1916.

qs.q: How many delegates attended the first session of the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: Seventy-two delegates met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, in December 1885.

qs.q: The Surat session of 1907, at which the Congress split, was presided over by:
qs.e: Rash Behari Ghosh was the Moderates' choice as president, and the Extremists' opposition broke up the session.

qs.q: The Lucknow session of 1916, which saw the Congress reunite, was presided over by:
qs.e: Ambica Charan Majumdar presided when the Moderates and Extremists reunited and the Lucknow Pact was signed.

qs.q: Who started the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals to spread nationalist feeling?
qs.e: Tilak began the Ganapati festival in 1893 and the Shivaji festival in 1895.

qs.q: Who was the youngest ever President of the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: Azad presided at 35 in 1923 and was also president for the longest stretch, from 1940 to 1946.

qs.q: Who was the President of the Indian National Congress at the time of Independence in 1947?
qs.e: J. B. Kripalani held the office in 1947; Azad's long term had ended in 1946.

qs.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was popularly summed up in the phrase:
qs.e: The Act allowed detention without trial, hence the phrase. 'A post-dated cheque' was Gandhi's verdict on the Cripps Mission.

qs.q: The first all-India hartal against the Rowlatt Act was observed on:
qs.e: Gandhi called the hartal for 6 April 1919; the Jallianwala Bagh firing followed on 13 April.

qs.q: Which commission was appointed to enquire into the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
qs.e: The Hunter Commission of 1919 enquired into the Punjab disturbances; the Peel Commission had reorganised the army in 1859.

qs.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was formally approved at the Congress session held at:
qs.e: The Calcutta special session of September 1920 adopted it and the Nagpur session of December 1920 confirmed it.

qs.q: Gandhi offered his first satyagraha anywhere in the world in 1906 in:
qs.e: His first satyagraha was at Johannesburg against the Asiatic Registration Act; Champaran in 1917 was the first in India.

qs.q: The Nehru Report of 1928, which demanded dominion status, was prepared under the chairmanship of:
qs.e: Motilal Nehru headed the committee that drafted it as an Indian answer to the Simon Commission.

qs.q: The Hindustan Republican Association was founded in 1924 at:
qs.e: Sachindra Nath Sanyal, Ramprasad Bismil and Jogesh Chatterjee founded it at Kanpur; it became the HSRA in 1928.

qs.q: Jatin Das died in jail in 1929 after a hunger strike lasting:
qs.e: Jatindra Nath Das fasted for 63 days in Lahore jail demanding better treatment for political prisoners.

qs.q: J. P. Saunders was shot dead in December 1928 in revenge for the death of:
qs.e: Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Azad killed Saunders after Lajpat Rai died of injuries from a lathi charge.

qs.q: Subhas Chandra Bose escaped from India in 1941 travelling under the assumed name:
qs.e: He left Calcutta as the Pathan 'Ziauddin' and reached Germany through Kabul.

qs.q: Who hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank after the Quit India arrests?
qs.e: Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag, while Usha Mehta ran the underground Congress Radio.

qs.q: The Interim Government headed by Jawaharlal Nehru was formed on:
qs.e: It took office on 2 September 1946, and the Muslim League joined it in October.

qs.q: The Charter Act of 1833 added a Law Member to the Governor-General's Council; the first to hold the post was:
qs.e: Macaulay became Law Member and headed the first Law Commission; his 1835 Minute brought in English education.

qs.q: The first Indian to be appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council was:
qs.e: S. P. Sinha was appointed after the Morley-Minto reforms of 1909.

qs.q: Which Act separated Burma from India?
qs.e: The 1935 Act separated Burma, created provincial autonomy and set up the RBI and a Federal Court.

qs.q: Which Act introduced indirect elections to the legislative councils for the first time?
qs.e: The 1892 Act allowed members to be recommended by local bodies and permitted budget discussion.

qs.q: The Kol rebellion of 1831 was led by:
qs.e: Buddho Bhagat led the Kol rising in Chhotanagpur; Birsa Munda's Ulgulan came in 1899–1900.

qs.q: The Indigo revolt of 1859–60 in Bengal was led by:
qs.e: The Biswas brothers led the ryots of Nadia; Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan exposed the planters.

qs.q: India's first newspaper, Hicky's Bengal Gazette, was published in 1780 from:
qs.e: James Augustus Hicky printed it in Calcutta; it is also called the Calcutta General Advertiser.

qs.q: Who is known as the 'liberator of the Indian press'?
qs.e: Metcalfe repealed the 1823 licensing rules in 1835. Ripon only repealed the Vernacular Press Act; Lytton passed it.

qs.q: Which newspaper changed overnight from Bengali to English to escape the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
qs.e: Founded in 1868 by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh, it slipped out of the Act, which covered only Indian-language papers.

qs.q: The Urdu weekly Al-Hilal was started in 1912 by:
qs.e: Azad published it from Calcutta; after it was banned in 1914 he started Al-Balagh. Mohammad Ali's paper was Comrade.

qs.q: The English weekly 'Comrade' was started by:
qs.e: Mohammad Ali started Comrade in 1911 and the Urdu Hamdard later; Azad's paper was Al-Hilal.

qs.q: Which of these papers was NOT published by Mahatma Gandhi?
qs.e: Kesari was Tilak's Marathi paper. Gandhi ran Young India (English), Navajivan (Gujarati) and Harijan.

qs.q: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was repealed in 1882 by:
qs.e: Lytton passed the 'gagging act' and Ripon repealed it, in keeping with his liberal reputation.

qs.q: The English daily 'Bande Mataram' (1906), voice of the Extremists, was started by Bipin Chandra Pal and edited by:
qs.e: Aurobindo Ghosh edited it from Calcutta. Do not confuse the paper with Bankim Chandra's song of the same name.

qs.q: The newspaper 'The Bengalee' is associated with:
qs.e: Surendranath Banerjee edited it from 1879 and was jailed for contempt of court in 1883.

qs.q: The Hindu was started in 1878 at:
qs.e: G. Subramania Iyer and M. Veeraraghavachariar started it in Madras, the same year as the Vernacular Press Act.

qs.q: Bombay Samachar, one of the oldest newspapers in Asia, is published in:
qs.e: Fardunjee Marzban started it in 1822 in Gujarati, and it is still published.

qs.q: Mirat-ul-Akhbar, a paper of Raja Ram Mohan Roy, was published in:
qs.e: Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822) was in Persian; his Sambad Kaumudi was in Bengali.

qs.q: The Calcutta Madrasa was founded in 1781 by:
qs.e: Hastings set it up for Persian and Arabic learning; Jonathan Duncan founded the Sanskrit College at Benares in 1791.

qs.q: The Sanskrit College at Benares was founded in 1791 by:
qs.e: Duncan, the British Resident at Benares, founded it. William Jones founded the Asiatic Society (1784).

qs.q: Macaulay's Minute on education, which made English the medium of higher education, was presented in:
qs.e: The Minute is dated 2 February 1835 and Bentinck accepted it. 1813 was the Charter Act grant; 1854 was Wood's Despatch.

qs.q: The Hunter Commission on education (1882) was appointed during the viceroyalty of:
qs.e: W. W. Hunter's commission studied primary and secondary education. The Hunter Committee of 1919 on Jallianwala Bagh is a different body.

qs.q: The Indian Universities Act of 1904 followed the recommendations of the:
qs.e: Curzon appointed Thomas Raleigh's commission in 1902; the Act tightened government control over universities.

qs.q: The Sadler Commission (1917–19) was appointed to study the problems of:
qs.e: It is also called the Calcutta University Commission and proposed a 12-year school course.

qs.q: The Hartog Committee of 1929 was set up as an auxiliary committee of the:
qs.e: It reported on education and warned of 'wastage and stagnation' in primary schooling.

qs.q: The central idea of the Wardha scheme of Basic Education (1937) was:
o: English as the medium of instruction
University education on the London model
qs.e: Gandhi's Nai Talim, worked out by the Zakir Hussain committee, built seven years of free schooling around a craft.

qs.q: The Sargent Plan of 1944 aimed at:
o: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14
Setting up universities in the three presidency towns
Replacing English with Persian in courts
Giving primary education to municipal boards
qs.e: John Sargent's plan set a 40-year target for universal schooling of children aged 6 to 14.

qs.q: Arrange in chronological order: Wood's Despatch, Macaulay's Minute, Sadler Commission, Hunter Commission.
o: Macaulay's Minute, Wood's Despatch, Hunter Commission, Sadler Commission
Wood's Despatch, Macaulay's Minute, Hunter Commission, Sadler Commission
Macaulay's Minute, Hunter Commission, Wood's Despatch, Sadler Commission
Macaulay's Minute, Wood's Despatch, Sadler Commission, Hunter Commission
qs.e: 1835, 1854, 1882 and 1917. The mnemonic: My Wise Hunter Rides Swiftly.

qs.q: Arrange these press laws in chronological order: Indian Press Act, Vernacular Press Act, Metcalfe's Act, Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act.
o: Metcalfe's Act, Vernacular Press Act, Newspapers Act, Indian Press Act
Vernacular Press Act, Metcalfe's Act, Newspapers Act, Indian Press Act
Metcalfe's Act, Newspapers Act, Vernacular Press Act, Indian Press Act
Metcalfe's Act, Vernacular Press Act, Indian Press Act, Newspapers Act
qs.e: 1835, 1878, 1908 and 1910. The last two came under Minto II to curb the Swadeshi press.

qs.q: The Indian Press Act of 1910, which demanded security deposits from papers, was passed under:
qs.e: Minto II passed both the Newspapers Act (1908) and the Indian Press Act (1910); both were repealed in 1922.

qs.q: Rani Velu Nachiyar, who regained her kingdom from the Company in 1780, was the queen of:
qs.e: She won with Hyder Ali's help, long before 1857. Kittur was Chennamma's state and Ramgarh Avantibai's.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Kittur Rani Chennamma rose against the British in:
qs.e: She resisted in 1824 when the British refused to recognise her adopted son — 33 years before 1857.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Kittur, the kingdom of Rani Chennamma, is in present-day:
qs.e: Kittur is in Belagavi district, Karnataka; her ally was Sangolli Rayanna.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Bhikaji Cama unfurled an Indian flag in 1907 at the International Socialist Congress held at:
qs.e: She raised the flag at Stuttgart, Germany, on 22 August 1907; she lived in Paris.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Who ran the secret Congress Radio during the Quit India Movement?
qs.e: Usha Mehta broadcast from hiding in Bombay in 1942. Aruna Asaf Ali is the one who hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Matangini Hazra, 'Gandhi Buri', was shot in 1942 while leading a march on the police station at:
qs.e: She was 73 and fell holding the tricolour at Tamluk, Midnapore, in September 1942.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Kanaklata Barua, shot at the age of 17 during the Quit India Movement, belonged to:
qs.e: She was killed while trying to hoist the flag at the Gohpur police station, Assam. Matangini Hazra was from Bengal.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Who was India's first woman Chief Minister?
qs.e: Sucheta Kripalani became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1963. Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Who became the first woman Governor of an Indian state?
qs.e: Sarojini Naidu became Governor of the United Provinces in 1947; her daughter Padmaja later governed West Bengal.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Kasturba Gandhi died in detention in 1944 at:
qs.e: She and Gandhi were held at the Aga Khan Palace after the Quit India arrests; she died there on 22 February 1944.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Pritilata Waddedar led the 1932 attack on the:
qs.e: She led Surya Sen's group against the Pahartali club in Chittagong and took poison rather than be caught.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Which Indian woman was the first to contest an election to a legislature, in Madras in 1926?
qs.e: Kamaladevi contested and narrowly lost; Muthulakshmi Reddy was nominated, not elected, to the Madras Council the same year.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Rani Gaidinliu led a movement among the:
qs.e: She was jailed at 16 in 1932 and freed in 1947; Nehru gave her the title 'Rani'.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Tirot Sing, who fought the Anglo-Khasi war of 1829–33, was a chief of the:
qs.e: He was chief of Nongkhlaw in the Khasi hills; U Kiang Nongbah led the Jaintias in 1860–62.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: U Kiang Nongbah, hanged at Jowai in 1862, led a rising in the:
qs.e: He led the Jaintia revolt of 1860–62. Tirot Sing was the Khasi chief, three decades earlier.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: The Rampa rebellion of 1922–24 was led by:
qs.e: Alluri Sitarama Raju fought in the Godavari agency of Andhra against forest laws. Birsa Munda led the Ulgulan of 1899–1900.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Veer Narayan Singh is honoured as the first martyr of 1857 from:
qs.e: The zamindar of Sonakhan shared hoarded grain with the starving in 1856, joined the revolt and was hanged at Raipur.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Tilka Manjhi, an early Adivasi rebel against the Company, is associated with the region of:
qs.e: He led the hill people around Bhagalpur in the 1780s and is remembered for attacking Collector Augustus Cleveland.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: The Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (1906) was founded by:
qs.e: V.O.C., the 'Kappalottiya Tamizhan', ran ships from Tuticorin to challenge British shipping.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: In 1911 Vanchinathan shot which British official at Maniyachi railway station?
qs.e: Ashe was Collector of Tirunelveli. Kingsford was the Muzaffarpur target and Saunders was shot by Bhagat Singh's group.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Tirupur Kumaran is remembered as 'Kodi Kaatha Kumaran' because he:
o: Died holding the national flag during a march in 1932
Hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank
qs.e: He was beaten to death by police at Tirupur in 1932 but did not let the flag fall.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: To escape arrest in 1908, the poet Subramania Bharati moved to the French territory of:
qs.e: He lived in Pondicherry for about ten years and kept writing patriotic poems.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: The 'Ali brothers', leaders of the Khilafat movement, were:
qs.e: Mohammad Ali (Jauhar) and Shaukat Ali led the Khilafat movement with Gandhi; Mohammad Ali presided at Kakinada in 1923.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Hakim Ajmal Khan was one of the founders of:
qs.e: He helped found Jamia in 1920 during Non-Cooperation, and presided over the Ahmedabad Congress of 1921.
qs.tag: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle

qs.q: Who was the secretary of the States Ministry who helped Sardar Patel integrate the princely states?
qs.e: V. P. Menon later wrote 'The Story of the Integration of the Indian States'. Panikkar and Kunzru sat on the Fazl Ali Commission.

qs.q: Operation Polo (1948) was launched to integrate:
qs.e: The 'police action' of 13–17 September 1948 ended the Nizam's resistance. Goa was freed by Operation Vijay.

qs.q: Junagadh became part of India after:
o: Its Nawab signed the Instrument of Accession
qs.e: The Nawab had acceded to Pakistan and fled; the 1948 plebiscite went overwhelmingly for India.

qs.q: Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India on:
qs.e: He signed as tribal raiders from Pakistan advanced; Indian troops landed at Srinagar on 27 October.

qs.q: Goa was freed from Portuguese rule in December 1961 through:
qs.e: Goa, Daman and Diu became a Union Territory; Goa became a state only in 1987.

qs.q: Sikkim became the 22nd state of India in 1975 through the:
qs.e: The 35th Amendment had made it an 'associate state'; the 36th made it a full state.

qs.q: Potti Sriramulu died in 1952 while fasting for:
qs.e: His death forced the creation of Andhra State on 1 October 1953.

qs.q: Which was the first state formed on a linguistic basis after Independence?
qs.e: Andhra State came in 1953. Orissa (1936) was the first province formed on language, before Independence.

qs.q: Who among these was NOT a member of the States Reorganisation (Fazl Ali) Commission?
qs.e: Remember FPK. Pattabhi Sitaramayya was in the JVP Committee with Nehru and Patel.

qs.q: The JVP Committee on linguistic states (1948) consisted of:
o: Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya
Nehru, V. P. Menon and Panikkar
qs.e: JVP stands for Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai and Pattabhi; it too set language aside for the time being.

qs.q: The Dhar Commission of 1948 favoured reorganising provinces on the basis of:
qs.e: S. K. Dhar's commission rejected language as the main basis; the Fazl Ali Commission later accepted it broadly.

qs.q: The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created:
qs.e: It came into force on 1 November 1956. The Fazl Ali Commission had suggested 16 states and 3 territories.

qs.q: Maharashtra and Gujarat were formed out of Bombay State in:
qs.e: Both were created on 1 May 1960, which is celebrated as Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day.

qs.q: Haryana was carved out of Punjab in:
qs.e: Haryana was formed on 1 November 1966, and Chandigarh became a Union Territory.

qs.q: Nagaland became a state of India in:
